objection_hooks: If phonetic differences are irrelevant, how can precise meter be maintained in sacred chants
The claim that meaning remains unchanged may ignore subtle semantic nuances conveyed by the extra syllable
Equating words by reducing syllable count might undermine the significance of traditional nomenclature in ritual contexts

sanskrit: निधनमिति त्र्यक्षरं तत्सममेव भवति तानि ह वा एतानि द्वाविंशतिरक्षराणि
transliteration: nidhanamiti tryakṣaraṃ tatsamameva bhavati tāni ha vā etāni dvāviṃśatirakṣarāṇi
translation: The word nidhana has three syllables. All words, having three syllables each, are the same [when used in praise of the Sāma ]. All these together have twenty-two syllables.
word_meaning: Nidhanam iti tri-akṣaram, the word nidhana is three-syllabled; tat samam eva bhavati, that makes it the same [as the other three-syllabled words forming parts of the Sāma]; tāni ha vai etāni, all these together constitute; dvāviṃśatiḥ akṣarāṇi, twenty-two syllables.
commentary: There are seven ways of worshipping the Sāma: through hiṃkāra, prastāva, ādi, pratihāra, udgītha, upadrava, and nidhana. Taken together these words have twenty-two syllables. Taken separately each of them may be treated as three-syllabled and recited accordingly. They are therefore all equal for purposes of the Sāma worship.
contextual_topics: Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
claim_candidates: Three‑syllable words are treated as equivalent in Sāma worship
The seven worship terms together comprise twenty‑two syllables, suggesting a numerological pattern
Uniform three‑syllable recitation permits a standardized ritual format irrespective of semantic differences
The equivalence of three‑syllable terms implies that syllabic form outweighs literal meaning in the efficacy of Sāma worship
The classification of worship methods by syllable count reflects a symbolic system linking sound structure to sacred potency
objection_hooks: Does mere syllable count genuinely confer ritual equivalence, or does the semantic content of the words remain essential?
The significance of the total of twenty‑two syllables may be arbitrary rather than intrinsically meaningful.
Prioritizing form over content could diminish the expressive and devotional richness of the hymns.
Treating all three‑syllable terms as interchangeable might overlook contextual nuances required for proper worship.

sanskrit: एकविंशत्यादित्यमाप्नोत्येकविंशो वा इतोऽसावादित्यो द्वाविंशेन परमादित्याज्जयति तन्नाकं तद्विशोकम्
transliteration: ekaviṃśatyādityamāpnotyekaviṃśo vā ito'sāvādityo dvāviṃśena paramādityājjayati tannākaṃ tadviśokam
translation: With the help of those twenty-one syllables, one can attain the status of the sun [which is also Death]. The sun occupies the twenty-first place after the things that come between the earth and the sun [those things being the twelve months, the five seasons, and the three worlds]. One can then go beyond the sun if one knows the twenty-second syllable. That world is full of joy and free from all sorrows.
word_meaning: Ekaviṃśatyā, by twenty-one [syllables]; ādityam āpnoti, one attains union with the sun [because the sun marks the end of everything, and it is therefore death]; ekaviṃśaḥ vai, [the sun is] the twenty-first [after the twelve months, the five seasons, and the three worlds]; itaḥ, from this [world]; asau ādityaḥ, the sun over there; dvāviṃśena, by [knowing] the twenty-second [syllable]; ādityāt param jayati, one attains the next higher world from the sun; tat nākam, that [place is] joyful; tat viśokaṃ, that [place is] free from all suffering.
commentary: The Upaniṣad says that if you worship Sāma with these twenty-one syllables, you attain the sun, which is the same as death. But how is the number significant? It is significant because the sun occupies the twenty-first position after the things that intervene between the earth and the sun. According to the Vedas those things are the twelve months, the five seasons, and the three worlds. But if you worship the Sāma with twenty-two syllables, you then go beyond the sun. Where? To a place called Nāka, where there is only happiness and no suffering.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Mastery of the twenty-one sacred syllables leads to identification with the sun, which symbolizes death, indicating that ritual utterance can effect a transition to the state of death

The enumeration of twelve months, five seasons, and three worlds as intervening elements positions the sun as the twenty-first cosmic marker, implying a structured cosmological order that can be traversed through sound

Knowing the twenty-second syllable enables one to surpass the sun and reach a realm called Nāka, described as free of sorrow, suggesting that an additional syllable functions as a key to liberation beyond the cycle of death

The description of Nāka as a place of joy and absence of suffering constitutes an early textual reference to a liberated state akin to moksha, implying that liberation is attainable through specific phonetic practice
objection_hooks: How can a mere syllable, a linguistic unit, cause a metaphysical transition such as becoming the sun or death
The identification of the sun with death may be metaphorical; does the text intend a literal ontological equivalence, or is it symbolic of the dissolution of the ego

The claim that the twenty-second syllable grants access to a realm beyond the sun assumes a hierarchical cosmology; is there textual evidence that such a realm exists independently of the ritual context
Equating Nāka with moksha may be anachronistic; does the Upanishadic commentary explicitly link this joy-filled realm with liberation, or is that a later interpretive overlay

sanskrit: आप्नोती हादित्यस्य जयं परो हास्यादित्यजयाज्जयो भवति य एतदेवं विद्वानात्मसंमितमतिमृत्यु सप्तविधं सामोपास्ते सामोपास्ते
transliteration: āpnotī hādityasya jayaṃ paro hāsyādityajayājjayo bhavati ya etadevaṃ vidvānātmasaṃmitamatimṛtyu saptavidhaṃ sāmopāste sāmopāste
translation: If a person knows all about the Sāma, and performs the sevenfold Sāma worship, treating the Sāma as himself and as something beyond death, he wins the state of the sun and then wins a place even higher than the sun.
word_meaning: Āpnoti ha ādityasya jayam, one wins the state of the sun; paraḥ ha ādityajayāt asya jayaḥ bhavati, one wins a world even higher than the sun; yaḥ, one who; etat evam vidvān, knows this [Sāma] thus; ātmasammitam, as oneself; atimṛtyu saptavidham sāma upāste sāma upāste, performs the deathless sevenfold Sāma worship [the repetition marks the end of the section].
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: Mastery of the Sāma and its sevenfold worship guarantees attainment of the solar divine state
The sevenfold Sāma worship is characterized as deathless, implying it transcends ordinary mortality
Identifying the Sāma with one’s own self is a necessary condition for achieving a realm higher than the sun
The spiritual hierarchy described places the sun’s realm below a superior, ultimate state attainable through Sāma practice
objection_hooks: The causal link between ritual performance and becoming like the sun may be metaphorical rather than literal, challenging the claim of guaranteed attainment
The description of the worship as deathless raises the question of whether the text intends a literal escape from death or a symbolic overcoming of fear
Equating a hymn (Sāma) with the self could be a poetic device rather than an ontological identity, undermining the necessity of self-identification
The notion of a realm higher than the sun lacks clear definition, making the hierarchical claim ambiguous

sanskrit: मनो हिंकारो वाक्प्रस्तावश्चक्षुरुद्गीथः श्रोत्रं प्रतिहारः प्राणो निधनमेतद्गायत्रं प्राणेषु प्रोतम्
transliteration: mano hiṃkāro vākprastāvaścakṣurudgīthaḥ śrotraṃ pratihāraḥ prāṇo nidhanametadgāyatraṃ prāṇeṣu protam
translation: The mind is hiṃkāra, the organ of speech is the prastāva, the eyes are the udgītha, the ears are the pratihāra, and the vital breath [in its fine (five?) forms] is the nidhana . The Gāyatrī prayer is controlled by the vital breath.
word_meaning: Manaḥ hiṃkāraḥ, the mind is the hiṃkāra; vāk prastāvaḥ, the organ of speech is the prastāva; cakṣuḥ udgīthāḥ, the eyes are the udgītha; śrotram pratihāraḥ, the ears are the pratihāra; prāṇaḥ nidhanam, the vital breath is the nidhana; etāt gāyatram, this Gāyatrī prayer; prāṇeṣu protam, is rooted in the vital breath.
commentary: So long the fivefold and the sevenfold Sāma worships have been discussed, but the names of those worships have not been mentioned. Gāyatra is the first among them. Corresponding to the Gāyatra is the hiṃkāra, with which the worship begins. Similarly, in any act of worship, the mind may be regarded as the hiṃkāra, for it is the mind that must act first before all the other organs. Next to the mind is the organ of speech. A person first thinks and then speaks out his intentions. The organ of speech is therefore the prastāva. The eyes are the udgītha because of their importance. The ears are the pratihāra, for you can ‘turn away from’ things you don’t want to hear. Prāṇa, the vital breath, is the nidhana, for when you have suṣupti, dreamless sleep, all the organs merge into the vital breath. The Gāyatrī is worshipped as the vital breath. This is why the Sāma called Gāyatra is. said to be rooted in the vital breath.
contextual_topics: In Sleep One Reaches Being
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The mind (hiṃkāra) must act before speech, eyes, ears, and breath in any act of worship
The vital breath (prāṇa) is the ultimate substrate (nidhana) that unifies all sensory organs during deep, dreamless sleep
The Gāyatrī prayer is fundamentally controlled by the vital breath, indicating that breath is the operative principle of this mantra
The designation of the eyes as udgītha and ears as pratihāra reflects a functional hierarchy where vision is primary and hearing is secondary, capable of being turned away
objection_hooks: If breath underlies mental activity, how can the mind be said to act before breath?
The claim that breath unifies organs in dreamless sleep may be metaphorical; does it imply literal physiological merging?
Is the Gāyatrī not primarily a verbal utterance independent of respiration, challenging its control by breath?
Why privilege vision over hearing in the hierarchy of senses; could this be a cultural bias?

sanskrit: स एवमेतद्गायत्रं प्राणेषु प्रोतं वेद प्राणी भवति सर्वमायुरेति ज्योग्जीवति महान्प्रजया पशुभिर्भवति महान्कीर्त्या महामनाः स्यात्तद्व्रतम्
transliteration: sa evametadgāyatraṃ prāṇeṣu protaṃ veda prāṇī bhavati sarvamāyureti jyogjīvati mahānprajayā paśubhirbhavati mahānkīrtyā mahāmanāḥ syāttadvratam
translation: This Gāyatra Sāma is rooted in the prāṇas . He who knows this becomes full of vitality, has a long life, and his life is brilliant. Also, he is fortunate in his children, and he has many domestic animals. He is one of the most famous people. To be noble-minded is the aim of his life.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ, he who; evam, this way; etat gāyatram, this Gāyatra Sāma; prāṇeṣu protam, rooted in the prāṇas; veda, knows; prāṇī, with life; bhavati, is endowed; sarvam āyuḥ, the full span of life; eti, attains; jyok jīvati, a bright [life]; mahān prajayā, great in progeny; paśubhiḥ, [and] animals; bhavati, becomes [rich with]; mahān kīrtyā, with a good reputation; mahāmanāḥ syāt, is noble in character; tat vratam, that is the aim of his life.
commentary: Whoever knows that the Sāma named Gāyatra is based on the prāṇas is truly alive—that is, all his organs are strong and healthy and he is never physically handicapped. The full span of a person’s life is said to be a hundred years. A person who worships the Sāma lives that long. And he lives a wonderful life, able to influence many people. He is respected as one of the greatest people in the world. He has many children and many domestic animals, but his sole aim in life is to have a large heart, without a trace of meanness in his mind.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Knowledge of the Gāyatra Sāma rooted in the prāṇas ensures that a person’s bodily organs remain strong and free from disability
Mastery of the Gāyatra Sāma guarantees a lifespan of up to one hundred years
The practice of the Gāyatra Sāma leads to material prosperity manifested as numerous offspring and domestic animals
The ultimate purpose of a life devoted to the Gāyatra Sāma is the cultivation of a noble generous mind devoid of meanness
The benefits of health longevity and prosperity are contingent upon intellectual knowledge of the hymn rather than ritual performance
objection_hooks: How can mere intellectual knowledge of a hymn causally produce physical health and the absence of disability without any observable mechanism
The claim of a guaranteed hundred year lifespan lacks empirical evidence does scriptural authority alone suffice to establish such a precise lifespan
Equating attainment of material wealth and many children with spiritual practice may conflict with Advaita’s emphasis on renunciation of worldly attachments
If the aim of life is a noble mind why does the verse also stress external prosperity suggesting a mixed agenda that could dilute the pursuit of inner virtue

sanskrit: अभिमन्थति स हिंकारो धूमो जायते स प्रस्तावो ज्वलति स उद्गीथोऽङ्गारा भवन्ति स प्रतिहार उपशाम्यति तन्निधनं संशाम्यति तन्निधनमेतद्रथंतरमग्नौ प्रोतम्
transliteration: abhimanthati sa hiṃkāro dhūmo jāyate sa prastāvo jvalati sa udgītho'ṅgārā bhavanti sa pratihāra upaśāmyati tannidhanaṃ saṃśāmyati tannidhanametadrathaṃtaramagnau protam
translation: When one rubs two pieces of wood against each other to light a fire, that is the hiṃkāra. When it produces smoke, that is the prastāva . Then when the flame appears, that is the udgītha . The charcoals that result are the pratihāra, and when the fire begins to go out, that is the nidhana . When the flame is completely extinguished, that also is the nidhana. This Sāma called Rathantara is rooted in fire.
word_meaning: Abhimanthati, rubbing [one piece of wood against another to produce fire]; saḥ hiṃkāraḥ, that is the hiṃkāra; dhūmaḥ jāyate, the smoke it produces; saḥ prastāvaḥ, that is the prastāva; jvalati, the flames that appear; saḥ udgīthaḥ, that is the udgītha; aṅgārāḥ bhavanti, the charcoals that result; saḥ pratihāraḥ, that is the pratihāra; upaśāmyati, when the fire begins to go out; tat nidhanam, that is the nidhana; saṃśāmyati, when the fire is completely extinguished; tat nidhanam, that [also] is the nidhana; etat rathantaram, this [Sāma] called Rathantara; agnau protam, is rooted in fire.
commentary: The rubbing of two pieces of wood together to produce fire is the hiṃkāra, for that is the beginning of the fire. And the smoke that results is the prastāva, for both are likely to continue. When the fire bursts into flame, that is the udgītha, because when there are flames the oblations are offered into them for the gods and goddesses. This is why this part is superior and why the flames are called the udgītha. The charcoals that are formed are called the pratihāra, for the charcoals are collected for future use. Upaśām means the process of subsiding—that is, the fire begins to subside but does not quite go out. Then the word saṃśām means ‘completely extinguished.’ The fire is then dead, so it is like the nidhana (death). The Rathantara Sāma is said to be based on fire, for when fire is being produced by rubbing the two sticks, the Rathantara Sāma is recited.
contextual_topics: The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: The frictional rubbing of two sticks (hiṃkāra) marks the initiation of sacrificial activity
The emergence of smoke (prastāva) signifies the continuity of ritual offering beyond the initial act
The flame (udgītha) is regarded as superior because it serves as the medium for offering oblations to the deities
The charcoals (pratihāra) are retained for future use, indicating that ritual remnants can be conserved for subsequent rites
The complete extinguishing of fire (nidhana) is equated with death, implying that the cessation of ritual activity symbolizes the end of spiritual vitality
objection_hooks: How can the physical process of friction be legitimately interpreted as a symbol for sacrificial initiation when the verse merely describes a practical method without explicit symbolic language?
Does the persistence of smoke truly represent continuity of ritual, or is it simply a natural byproduct without theological significance?
Why should the flame be considered superior to other stages when all stages are necessary for the fire's existence; does the commentary's preference reflect a bias rather than an inherent hierarchy?
Is equating the extinguishing of fire with death metaphorically appropriate, or does it conflate physical cessation with spiritual termination without textual justification?

sanskrit: स य एवमेतद्रथंतरमग्नौ प्रोतं वेद ब्रह्मवर्चस्यन्नादो भवति सर्वमायुरेति ज्योग्जीवति महान्प्रजया पशुभिर्भवति महान्कीर्त्या न प्रत्यङ्ङग्निमाचामेन्न निष्ठीवेत्तद्व्रतम्
transliteration: sa ya evametadrathaṃtaramagnau protaṃ veda brahmavarcasyannādo bhavati sarvamāyureti jyogjīvati mahānprajayā paśubhirbhavati mahānkīrtyā na pratyaṅṅagnimācāmenna niṣṭhīvettadvratam
translation: He who knows that this Rathantara Sāma is rooted in fire, acquires the kind of glow that Vedic scholarship produces. He also enjoys eating. He lives the full span of his life, and his life is brilliant. He is well known for his children and for his animal wealth, and he commands great respect in society. His vow is that he will never eat with fire in front of him and he will never spit.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ evam etat rathantaram agnau protam veda, he who knows that this Rathantara Sāma is rooted in fire; brahmavarcasī, acquires the glow that Vedic knowledge gives; annādaḥ bhavati, he enjoys eating food; sarvam āyuḥ eti, he lives the full span of his life; jyok jīvati, he lives a bright life; mahān prajayā paśubhiḥ bhavati, he distinguishes himself by his children and by the animal wealth he acquires; mahān kīrtyā, his reputation spreads far and wide; tat vratam, his principle is; na pratyak agnim ācāmet, never to
commentary: By his moral character and his scholarship in the Vedas, he acquires a radiance about him. [The underlying thought in these two mantras is that everything a person does is spiritual. This includes even physical experiences.]
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: He who combines moral character with Vedic scholarship attains a radiant reputation that enhances his social standing
The vow to never eat with fire and never spit is presented as a means to preserve spiritual purity
Living according to Vedic principles is said to result in a full lifespan and a brilliant life
Distinction by having many children and animal wealth is portrayed as an indicator of spiritual success
The commentary asserts that every physical action, including eating, carries spiritual significance
objection_hooks: The link between moral character and social radiance may be coincidental, as material success alone can produce reputation
The prohibition against eating with fire appears arbitrary; why should this specific act affect spiritual purity
Equating progeny and animal wealth with spiritual achievement conflicts with teachings that advocate non‑attachment
Asserting that all physical actions are spiritual could be seen as overextending the concept beyond its doctrinal limits

sanskrit: उपमन्त्रयते स हिंकारो ज्ञपयते स प्रस्तावः स्त्रिया सह शेते स उद्गीथः प्रति स्त्रीं सह शेते स प्रतिहारः कालं गच्छति तन्निधनं पारं गच्छति तन्निधनमेतद्वामदेव्यं मिथुने प्रोतम्
transliteration: upamantrayate sa hiṃkāro jñapayate sa prastāvaḥ striyā saha śete sa udgīthaḥ prati strīṃ saha śete sa pratihāraḥ kālaṃ gacchati tannidhanaṃ pāraṃ gacchati tannidhanametadvāmadevyaṃ mithune protam
word_meaning: test, remove me.

sanskrit: उद्यन्हिंकार उदितः प्रस्तावो मध्यंदिन उद्गीथोऽपराह्णः प्रतिहारोऽस्तं यन्निधनमेतद्बृहदादित्ये प्रोतम्
transliteration: udyanhiṃkāra uditaḥ prastāvo madhyaṃdina udgītho'parāhṇaḥ pratihāro'staṃ yannidhanametadbṛhadāditye protam
translation: The rising sun is the hiṃkāra, the sun that has already risen is the prastāva, the midday sun is the udgītha, the afternoon sun is the pratihāra, and the setting sun is the nidhana . This Sāma called Bṛhat is based on the sun.
word_meaning: Udyan, the rising sun; hiṃkāraḥ, [is] the hiṃkāra; uditaḥ, the sun that has already risen; prastāvaḥ, [is] the prastāva; madhyandina, the midday sun; udgīthaḥ, [is] the udgītha; aparāhṇaḥ, the afternoon sun; pratihāraḥ, [is] the pratihāra; yat astam, that which is setting; nidhanam, [is] the nidhana; etat bṛhat,
commentary: The rising sun is the hiṃkāra, for that is the time when we first see the sun. When the sun has risen it is the prastāva, for that is when people start performing their daily religious riteṣ and rituals. The midday sun is the udgītha, because that is the best time of the day. Then the afternoon sun is the pratihāra, because that is the time when cattle are driven back home. And the setting sun is the nidhana, for at night domestic animals are kept confined in their pens. This Bṛhat Sāma is based on the sun, because the sun is its presiding deity.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
claim_candidates: The sun's phases are metaphorically linked to specific ritual times
The sun functions as the presiding deity of the Bṛhat Sāma, indicating that natural phenomena can serve as divine focal points in Vedic worship
The classification of the sun into hiṃkāra, prastāva, udgītha, pratihāra, and nidhana reflects a structured cosmological order that aligns human activities with celestial cycles
The naming of the Sāma after the sun suggests that musical compositions are intended to embody and honor cosmic principles
objection_hooks: The correlation between sun phases and ritual times may be culturally specific and not universally applicable
Interpreting the sun as a deity could be an anthropomorphic projection rather than a theological assertion
The structured classification might be a poetic device rather than evidence of an actual cosmological order
Naming a Sāma after the sun does not necessarily imply intentional embodiment of cosmic principles, as artistic motives may differ

sanskrit: स य एवमेतद्बृहदादित्ये प्रोतं वेद तेजस्व्यन्नादो भवति सर्वमायुरेति ज्योग्जीवति महान्प्रजया पशुभिर्भवति महान्कीर्त्या तपन्तं न निन्देत्तद्व्रतम्
transliteration: sa ya evametadbṛhadāditye protaṃ veda tejasvyannādo bhavati sarvamāyureti jyogjīvati mahānprajayā paśubhirbhavati mahānkīrtyā tapantaṃ na nindettadvratam
translation: He who knows that the Sāma called Bṛhat is rooted in the sun is spirited and has a great appetite. He lives the full span of his life, has a brilliant career, and is renowned for his children and for his animal wealth. His success in life brings him much fame. The vow he observes is that he will never utter a word against the sun, which gives us heat.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ evam etat bṛhat āditye protam veda, he who knows that the Sāma called Bṛhat is rooted in the sun; tejasvi, is spirited; annādaḥ bhavati, has a great appetite; sarvam āyuḥ etḥ lives the full span of his life; jyok jīvati, has a brilliant life; mahān prajayā paśubhiḥ bhavati, becomes famous for his children and for his animal wealth; mahān kīrtyā, is highly respected; tapantam na nindet, he never uses a bad word against the hot sun; tat vratam, that is his vow.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Knowing that the Sāma Bṛhat is rooted in the sun confers vigor and a great appetite
Observing a vow never to speak ill of the sun ensures a full lifespan and fame
Reverence toward the sun is linked to material prosperity such as numerous children and animal wealth
The sun is presented as a moral authority whose heat warrants respect and silence
objection_hooks: The causal link between knowledge of a song’s origin and physical vigor is not logically established
Longevity and fame may result from other factors; the vow’s effect could be coincidental
Material prosperity might depend on social or economic conditions, not merely reverence of the sun
Assigning moral authority to a natural body may be anthropomorphic and lacks philosophical justification

sanskrit: अभ्राणि सम्प्लवन्ते स हिंकारो मेघो जायते स प्रस्तावो वर्षति स उद्गीथो विद्योतते स्तनयति स प्रतिहार उद्गृह्णाति तन्निधनमेतद्वैरूपं पर्जन्ये प्रोतम्
transliteration: abhrāṇi samplavante sa hiṃkāro megho jāyate sa prastāvo varṣati sa udgītho vidyotate stanayati sa pratihāra udgṛhṇāti tannidhanametadvairūpaṃ parjanye protam
translation: When light clouds consolidate, that is the hiṃkāra. When clouds likely to pour rain collect, that is the prastāva . When the rain begins, that is the udgītha . Then there are flashes of lightning and the roar of thunder. This is the pratihāra . When it all stops, that is the nidhana . This Sāma called Vairūpa is rooted in the clouds.
word_meaning: Abhrāṇi, light clouds [bearing water]; saṃplavante, when they consolidate; saḥ hiṃkāraḥ, that is the hiṃkāra; meghaḥ jāyate, when clouds likely to pour rain appear; saḥ prastāvaḥ, that is the prastāva; varṣati saḥ udgīthaḥ, when it starts raining that is the udgītha; vidyotate, when lightning flashes; stanayati, [and] thunder roars; saḥ pratihāraḥ, that is the pratihāra; ut gṛhṇāti, when everything is over; tat nidhanam, that is the nidhana; etat vairūpam, this [Sāma called] Vairūpa; parjanye protam, is rooted in the clouds.
commentary: The word abhra means a cloud which bears ap, water. A cloud that pours rain is called megha . The English word ‘cloud’ is actually in Sanskrit parjanya . Abhra, megha, parjanya —these different names all mean cloud, but indicate the cloud in a different state. This is why the cloud is described here as vairūpa, with different forms. It is the sun that produces the cloud, and this is why the Sāma is first worshipped as the sun and then as the cloud.
contextual_topics: Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The sequential stages of cloud formation (abhra, megha, parjanya) illustrate that Brahman manifests in multiple transient forms while remaining the same underlying reality
The worship of the sun followed by the cloud demonstrates a progressive approach to divine worship, moving from a visible source to its subtle manifestation
Identifying the cloud as Vairūpa (various forms) suggests that ritual symbols can serve as substitutes for direct worship of the ultimate reality
The description of natural phenomena (rain, lightning, thunder) as stages of a single entity implies that the material world is an expression of a single divine principle
The cessation of the storm (nidhana) represents the dissolution of forms back into the unmanifest Brahman
objection_hooks: The claim that cloud stages represent Brahman's multiple forms may conflate metaphor with ontological identity, lacking explicit scriptural assertion
The idea that worship of sun then cloud is a progressive hierarchy could be challenged as merely reflecting ritual sequence, not theological progression
Asserting that ritual symbols substitute for direct worship may ignore the necessity of actual sacrificial rites prescribed elsewhere
Interpreting the storm's cessation as dissolution into Brahman may impose a metaphysical reading not intended in the verse's literal description of weather

sanskrit: स य एवमेतद्वैरूपं पर्जन्ये प्रोतं वेद विरूपांश्च सुरूपंश्च पशूनवरुन्धे सर्वमायुरेति ज्योग्जीवति महान्प्रजया पशुभिर्भवति महान्कीर्त्या वर्षन्तं न निन्देत्तद्व्रतम्
transliteration: sa ya evametadvairūpaṃ parjanye protaṃ veda virūpāṃśca surūpaṃśca paśūnavarundhe sarvamāyureti jyogjīvati mahānprajayā paśubhirbhavati mahānkīrtyā varṣantaṃ na nindettadvratam
translation: He who knows that this Sāma called Vairūpa has its source in the clouds comes to acquire a large variety of animals, and all beautiful animals too. He has a long and brilliant life, and his children and animals are such that he becomes famous for them. His achievements also mark him as a great person.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ evam etat vairūpam parjanye protam veda, he who knows that this [Sāma called] Vairūpa is rooted in the clouds; virūpān ca surūpān ca paśūn avarundhe, he comes to possess a large variety of animals and beautiful animals also; sarvam āyuḥ eti, he lives the full span of his life; jyok jīvati, he has a brilliant life; mahān prajayā paśubhiḥ bhavati, he becomes famous for his children and for his animal wealth; mahān kīrtyā, he is renowned for his achievements; varṣantam na nindet tat vratam, his vow is not to criticize the clouds that pour rain.
commentary: It is a characteristic of those who worship the Sāma that they never find fault with others. This is why they do not say anything bad about even the clouds that give rain.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: He who refrains from criticizing clouds is presented as a hallmark of true worship of Sāma
The verse links knowledge of Vairūpa’s cloud origin with the acquisition of many animals and fame
It suggests that ethical restraint, such as not disparaging clouds, leads to a long and brilliant life
The vow not to denigrate the rain‑giving clouds is portrayed as essential for attaining prosperity and renown
objection_hooks: How does merely avoiding criticism of clouds causally produce material wealth and fame?
Is the promised acquisition of animals and reputation a literal outcome or a metaphorical illustration?
Does the text prescribe ethical non‑criticism as a substitute for ritual, or merely describe a trait of already successful individuals?
Could the injunction against speaking ill of clouds be symbolic rather than a literal prerequisite for success?

sanskrit: वसन्तो हिंकारो ग्रीष्मः प्रस्तावो वर्षा उद्गीथः शरत्प्रतिहारो हेमन्तो निधनमेतद्वैराजमृतुषु प्रोतम्
transliteration: vasanto hiṃkāro grīṣmaḥ prastāvo varṣā udgīthaḥ śaratpratihāro hemanto nidhanametadvairājamṛtuṣu protam
translation: Spring is the hiṃkāra, summer the prastāva, the rainy season the udgītha, autumn the pratihāra, and winter the nidhana . This Sāma known as Vairāja is rooted in the seasons.
word_meaning: Vasantaḥ hiṃkāraḥ, spring is the hiṃkāra; grīṣmaḥ prastāvaḥ, summer is the prastāva; varṣāḥ udgīthaḥ, the rainy season is the udgītha; śarat pratihāraḥ, autumn is the pratihāra; hemantaḥ nidhanam, winter is the nidhana; etat vairājam, this [Sāma called] Vairāja; ṛtuṣu protam, is rooted in the seasons.
commentary: The clouds determine the seasons. This is why the Sāma is first worshipped as the clouds and after that as the seasons.
claim_candidates: The classification of the five seasons as hiṃkāra, prastāva, udgītha, pratihāra, and nidhanam reflects a systematic symbolic ordering of natural cycles
The Sāma called Vairāja is conceptually rooted in the cyclical pattern of the seasons
The commentary asserts that clouds are the determining factor of seasonal change
The worship sequence of the Sāma, first as clouds and then as seasons, indicates a hierarchical ritual progression from atmospheric phenomena to temporal cycles
objection_hooks: The identification of seasons with specific terms may be merely linguistic labeling without deeper symbolic significance
Attributing the causality of seasonal change to clouds oversimplifies natural processes and may be metaphorical rather than literal
The notion of a ritual progression from clouds to seasons could be a conventional practice lacking philosophical import
The claim that Vairāja is rooted in the seasons may ignore alternative mythological or theological origins

sanskrit: स य एवमेतद्वैराजमृतुषु प्रोतं वेद विराजति प्रजया पशुभिर्ब्रह्मवर्चसेन सर्वमायुरेति ज्योग्जीवति महान्प्रजया पशुभिर्भवति महान्कीर्त्यर्तून्न निन्देत्तद्व्रतम्
transliteration: sa ya evametadvairājamṛtuṣu protaṃ veda virājati prajayā paśubhirbrahmavarcasena sarvamāyureti jyogjīvati mahānprajayā paśubhirbhavati mahānkīrtyartūnna nindettadvratam
translation: He who knows that the Sāma called Vairāja is rooted in the seasons is surrounded by his children and animals and has a radiance about him which is born of Vedic scholarship. He lives a long and brilliant life, and he is considered great for his children and for his animals. He is also highly respected for his great deeds. He follows the vow of never criticizing the seasons.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ evani etat vairājam ṛtuṣu protam veda, he who knows that this [Sāma called] Vairāja is rooted in the seasons; virājati, he lives; prajayā paśubhiḥ, surrounded by his children and animals; brahmavarcasena, he has the kind of radiance that is born of Vedic scholarship; sarvam āyuḥ eti, he lives the full span of his life; jyok jīvati, he lives a brilliant life; mahān prajayā paśubhiḥ bhavati, he is known to be great for his children and animals; mahān kīrtyā, he is famous for his deeds; ṛtūn na nindet tat vratam, his vow is that he will never criticize the seasons.
commentary: The person who knows that the Vairāja Sāma is rooted in the seasons becomes like the seasons himself. Each season has a beauty of its own. Similarly, this person has within him the beauty and grandeur of the good things he possesses, such as his wealth, good children, scholarship, and character. The rules of the Sāma forbid him from saying anything bad about the seasons, and he follows this.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Knowing the Vairāja Sāma as rooted in the seasons transforms a person into one who embodies the qualities of the seasons
Observing a vow of never criticizing the seasons leads to a long, brilliant, and respected life
The radiance derived from Vedic scholarship is a source of social esteem and material prosperity
Ethical restraint in speech, specifically not speaking ill of the seasons, is presented as a means to attain both personal longevity and communal honor
Association with children and animals signifies a moral duty that enhances one’s spiritual stature
objection_hooks: How can a mere vow about seasons causally affect lifespan?
Does the verse imply that the seasons have moral status, making criticism unethical, or is this a symbolic injunction?
Is the claim that Vedic scholarship radiance leads to material prosperity universally valid, or is it context‑specific?
Could the transformation into ‘like the seasons’ be metaphorical rather than literal, limiting its philosophical import?

sanskrit: पृथिवी हिंकारोऽन्तरिक्षं प्रस्तावो द्यौरुद्गीथो दिशः प्रतिहारः समुद्रो निधनमेताः शक्वर्यो लोकेषु प्रोताः
transliteration: pṛthivī hiṃkāro'ntarikṣaṃ prastāvo dyaurudgītho diśaḥ pratihāraḥ samudro nidhanametāḥ śakvaryo lokeṣu protāḥ
translation: The earth is the hiṃkāra, the space between the earth and heaven is the prastāva, heaven is the udgītha, the quarters are the pratihāra, and the ocean is the nidhana . The Sāma known as Śakvarī is rooted in the earth and other worlds.
word_meaning: Pṛthivī hiṃkāraḥ, the earth is the hiṃkāra; antarikṣam prastāvaḥ, the space between the earth and heaven is the prastāva; dyauḥ udgīthaḥ, heaven is the udgītha; diśaḥ pratihāraḥ, the quarters are the pratihāra; samudraḥ nidhanam, the ocean is the nidhana; etāḥ śakvaryaḥ lokeṣu protāḥ, these [the Sāma called] Śakvarī are rooted in the earth and other worlds.
commentary: If the seasons come and go, as they ought to, then things on the earth and the other worlds remain in balance. This is why the Sāma is first worshipped as the seasons and then as the worlds. But the question is: Sāma is singular. Why then has a plural word, śakvarī, been used here for the Sāma? Doesn’t it imply that there are many Sāmas ? No, the Sāma is always one and the same. There are not many Sāmas. The word śakvarī has a plural form, but it stands for the singular Sāma. Śaṅkara gives the example of the word revatī, which is similarly always used in the plural.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The verse identifies earth, space, heaven, quarters, and ocean as manifestations of the single hymn Śakvarī, indicating an underlying unity of all cosmic elements.
The plural form śakvarī applied to a singular Sāma shows that grammatical plurality can express ontological oneness in Vedic language.
By equating the hymn with the totality of creation, the text implies that sacred sound embodies the whole universe.
The commentary’s link between proper worship of the Sāma and the balance of seasons and worlds suggests that ritual practice sustains cosmic order.
objection_hooks: The identification of diverse cosmic elements with a single hymn may be metaphorical rather than ontological, challenging the claim of true unity.
Using a plural grammatical form for a singular deity could be a poetic convention, not a doctrinal statement of unity.
The assertion that worship of the Sāma causally maintains cosmic balance assumes ritual efficacy without empirical support.
Describing the intermediate space as prastāva might impose modern functional concepts onto ancient terminology, weakening the claim about its nature.

sanskrit: स य एवमेताः शक्वर्यो लोकेषु प्रोता वेद लोकी भवति सर्वमायुरेति ज्योग्जीवति महान्प्रजया पशुभिर्भवति महान्कीर्त्या लोकान्न निन्देत्तद्व्रतम्
transliteration: sa ya evametāḥ śakvaryo lokeṣu protā veda lokī bhavati sarvamāyureti jyogjīvati mahānprajayā paśubhirbhavati mahānkīrtyā lokānna nindettadvratam
translation: He who knows that the Sāma known as Śakvarī is located in the worlds goes to the best world. He also has a long and brilliant life and is well known for his children and for his animal wealth. He is considered to be a great person because of his great deeds. He takes a vow that he will never criticize the worlds.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ evam etāḥ śakvaryaḥ lokeṣu protāḥ veda, he who knows that these [i.e., the Sāma] known as Śakvarī are rooted in the worlds; lokī bhavati, goes to the best world; sarvam āyuḥ eti, lives the full span of his life; jyok jīvati, has a brilliant life; mahān prajayā paśubhiḥ bhavati, is well known for his children and for his animal wealth; mahān kīrtyā, is well known for his great deeds; lokān na nindet tat vratam, his vow is that he will never criticize the worlds.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: He who knows the Sāma Śakvarī and its presence in the worlds attains the best world
A long, brilliant life together with many children and animal wealth signifies great deeds and high reputation
Vowing never to criticize the worlds is presented as a moral commitment that enhances one’s standing
Possessing animal wealth (paśu) alongside human progeny contributes to a person’s greatness
objection_hooks: How can mere knowledge of a hymn guarantee passage to the best world without reference to ethical conduct?
Does longevity and brilliance necessarily indicate moral greatness, or could they be mere natural blessings?
Why is refraining from criticism of the worlds considered virtuous rather than a suppression of truth?
Is the emphasis on animal wealth ethically justified, or does it promote materialism?

sanskrit: अजा हिंकारोऽवयः प्रस्तावो गाव उद्गीथोऽश्वाः प्रतिहारः पुरुषो निधनमेता रेवत्यः पशुषु प्रोताः
transliteration: ajā hiṃkāro'vayaḥ prastāvo gāva udgītho'śvāḥ pratihāraḥ puruṣo nidhanametā revatyaḥ paśuṣu protāḥ
translation: Goats are the hiṃkāra, sheep are the prastāva, cows represent the udgītha, horses are the pratihāra, and a human being is the nidhana . The Sāma called Revatī is established in animals.
word_meaning: Ajāḥ hiṃkāraḥ, goats are the hiṃkāra; avayaḥ prastāvaḥ, sheep are the prastāva; gāvaḥ udgītha, cows are the udgītha; aśvāḥ pratihāraḥ, horses are the pratihāra; puruṣaḥ nidhanam, a human being is the nidhana; etāḥ revatyaḥ paśuṣu protāḥ, these [i.e., the Sāma known as] Revatī are established in animals.
commentary: Animals are useful to all the worlds. That is why, after worshipping the Sāma as the worlds, the worship as animals is suggested. As in the previous section in which the word śakvarī is always used in the plural (as śakvaryaḥ ), here also, the word revatī is always used in the plural ( revatyaḥ ).
contextual_topics: Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The classification of goats, sheep, cows, horses, and humans as hiṃkāra, prastāva, udgītha, pratihāra, and nidhana respectively indicates that each species embodies a distinct functional aspect of cosmic order

The commentary’s statement that animals are useful to all worlds supports the view that worship of the Sāma hymn can be extended from the cosmic realm to the animal realm as a progressive stage of devotion
The repeated plural usage of revatī in the text suggests that the Sāma hymn manifests collectively within multiple animals, implying a collective embodiment of the sacred sound
By equating the human being with nidhana, the verse implies that the ultimate purpose of human life is the cessation of individual existence, aligning with the Advaitic notion of merging into Brahman
Identifying specific animals with ritual terms serves as a symbolic substitute for performing actual sacrificial rites, allowing devotion through contemplation of animal forms
objection_hooks: Interpreting nidhana as "death" may impose a metaphysical meaning not explicit in the verse; the term could simply denote a ritual role rather than an existential purpose
The idea of progressive worship from worlds to animals is not explicitly stated in the commentary, which only mentions worship of animals after worship of worlds
The plural form revatī might be a grammatical convention rather than indicating a collective embodiment of the hymn
Suggesting that symbolic identification substitutes for literal sacrifice could be contested, as Vedic tradition emphasizes actual sacrificial acts rather than mere contemplation

sanskrit: स य एवमेता रेवत्यः पशुषु प्रोता वेद पशुमान्भवति सर्वमायुरेति ज्योग्जीवति महान्प्रजया पशुभिर्भवति महान्कीर्त्या पशून्न निन्देत्तद्व्रतम्
transliteration: sa ya evametā revatyaḥ paśuṣu protā veda paśumānbhavati sarvamāyureti jyogjīvati mahānprajayā paśubhirbhavati mahānkīrtyā paśūnna nindettadvratam
translation: He who knows that the Sāma called Revatī is rooted in animals acquires many animals. He has a long and brilliant life and becomes well known for his children and for his animal wealth. He also becomes a truly great person for his great deeds. His vow is that he will never say anything bad about animals.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ evam etaḥ revatyaḥ protāḥ veda, he who knows that these [i.e., the Sāma] called Revatī are rooted in animals; paśumān bhavati, comes to possess many animals; sarvam āyuḥ eti, lives the full span of his life; jyok jīvati, has a brilliant life; mahān prajayā paśubhiḥ bhavati, becomes a highly respected person because of his children and also his animal wealth; mahān kīrtyā, becomes a truly great person for his great deeds; paśūn na nindet tat vratam, he observes the vow of never saying anything bad about animals.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
The Three Branches of Duty
claim_candidates: Knowledge of the Sāma Revatī that animals are rooted in leads to acquisition of many animals and a long, brilliant life
Accumulating many children and animal wealth confers great reputation and fame
Observing a vow never to speak ill of animals is a hallmark of true greatness
One’s moral conduct toward animals determines the length of life and the extent of renown
objection_hooks: How can mere knowledge of a song guarantee the acquisition of animals and longevity?
The association between animal wealth and reputation may reflect cultural bias rather than a universal principle
A vow not to criticize animals alone may be insufficient for greatness without other virtues
The claim that conduct toward animals determines lifespan lacks empirical verification

sanskrit: लोम हिंकारस्त्वक्प्रस्तावो मांसमुद्गीथोस्थि प्रतिहारो मज्जा निधनमेतद्यज्ञायज्ञीयमङ्गेषु प्रोतम्
transliteration: loma hiṃkārastvakprastāvo māṃsamudgīthosthi pratihāro majjā nidhanametadyajñāyajñīyamaṅgeṣu protam
translation: Hair is the hiṃkāra, skin is the prastāva, flesh is the udgītha, bone is the pratihāra, and marrow is the nidhana . The Sāma called Yajñāyajñīya is spread all over the limbs of the body.
word_meaning: Loma hiṃkāraḥ, hair is the hiṃkāra; tvak prastāvaḥ, skin is the prastāva; māṃsam udgīthaḥ, flesh is the udgītha; asthi pratihāraḥ, bone is the pratihāra; majjā nidhanam, marrow is the nidhana; etat yajñāyajñīyam, this [Sāma called] Yajñāyajñīya; aṅgeṣu protam, is spread all over the limbs of the body.
commentary: We get much nourishment from animals to sustain our bodies. That is why, in the previous section, the Sāma has been worshipped in the animals, and now it is being worshipped in the various parts of the body. Hair is on top of the body, so it is given first place—the place given to the hiṃkāra when the Sāma is recited. Next to the hair is the skin. Similarly, next to the hiṃkāra is the prastāva. The flesh is the udgītha, for both are the most important part. Then the bones are the pratihāra, because after a body is cremated there will still be pieces of bone left, and these are ‘collected’ by the relatives. The marrow is the nidhana, for that is the end of everything.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The verse asserts that each bodily element (hair, skin, flesh, bone, marrow) corresponds to a specific ritual component (hiṃkāra, prastāva, udgītha, pratihāra, nidhana), making the human body itself a locus of sacred worship

The statement that the Sāma Yajñāyajñīya is spread over all limbs implies that internalizing the sacred chant replaces external animal offerings, indicating a shift from external ritual to internalized devotion
The commentary’s description of marrow as the ‘end of everything’ reflects a doctrinal view that the innermost part of the body represents the ultimate reality or Brahman
The ordering of body parts, beginning with hair (hiṃkāra) as the highest, conveys a hierarchical valuation of bodily constituents in relation to spiritual significance
The identification of body parts with ritual terms suggests that the self (Atman) is not separate from the ritual cosmos, supporting the non‑dual view of the self identical with Brahman
objection_hooks: The correlation between body parts and ritual terms may be metaphorical rather than literal, questioning whether the verse truly intends to sanctify the body
The claim that internalizing Sāma replaces animal sacrifice assumes a doctrinal shift not explicitly stated; the text may simply describe a parallel rather than a substitution
Interpreting marrow as representing ultimate reality could be an overextension; the commentary may refer to the physical end rather than a metaphysical Brahman
The hierarchical ordering might reflect practical considerations of ritual sequence rather than spiritual hierarchy, challenging the claim of spiritual valuation

sanskrit: स य एवमेतद्यज्ञायज्ञीयमङ्गेषु प्रोतं वेदाङ्गी भवति नाङ्गेन विहूर्छति सर्वमायुरेति ज्योग्जीवति महान्प्रजया पशुभिर्भवति महान्कीर्त्या संवत्सरं मज्ज्ञो नाश्नीयात्तद्व्रतं मज्ज्ञो नाश्नीयादिति वा
transliteration: sa ya evametadyajñāyajñīyamaṅgeṣu protaṃ vedāṅgī bhavati nāṅgena vihūrchati sarvamāyureti jyogjīvati mahānprajayā paśubhirbhavati mahānkīrtyā saṃvatsaraṃ majjño nāśnīyāttadvrataṃ majjño nāśnīyāditi vā
translation: He who knows that the Sāma known as Yajñāyajñīya is located in different parts of the body becomes possessed of a firm body and none of his organs has any defect. He has a long and brilliant life; and he becomes great because of his children and his animal wealth. He also becomes famous for his great deeds. His vow is that he will not eat meat for one whole year, or he will not eat it at all.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ evam etat yajñāyajñīyam aṅgeṣu protam veda, he who knows that this Sāma called Yajñāyajñīya is located in the different parts of the body; aṅgī bhavati, has a firm body; na aṅgena vihūrchati, has no defect in his limbs or organs; sarvam āyuḥ eti, he lives the full span of his life; jyok jīvati, he has a brilliant life; mahān prajayā paśubhiḥ bhavati, he becomes great in respect of his children and his animal wealth; mahān kīrtyā, he becomes great because of his great deeds; saṃvatsaram, for one whole year; majjñaḥ, meat; na aśnīyāt, will not eat; majjñaḥ na aśnīyāt iti vā, or will not eat meat at all; tat vratam, this is his vow.
commentary: ‘A firm body’ means a good, sound body with none of its organs or limbs defective. Even his nails and his hair will be normal. The word majjña, meat, is in the plural here. This implies that both fish and meat should be avoided.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: He who knows the internal Sāma Yajñāyajñīya located in the body attains a firm, defect‑free physical form
Abstaining from meat for a year or permanently leads to an extended and brilliant lifespan
The vow of meat abstinence also brings material prosperity, many children, animal wealth and fame for great deeds
The plural form of majjña indicates that the vow prohibits consumption of both meat and fish
objection_hooks: How can mere knowledge of a hymn situated in the body guarantee physical health without empirical evidence
Is the correlation between meat abstinence and longevity causally established or could other factors explain the extended life
Does the promise of material prosperity and fame rely on divine guarantee or is it a rhetorical incentive that may not hold universally
The interpretation that the plural majjña includes fish may be linguistically debatable; could the plural simply refer to multiple kinds of meat

sanskrit: अग्निर्हिंकारो वायुः प्रस्ताव आदित्य उद्गीथो नक्षत्राणि प्रतिहारश्चन्द्रमा निधनमेतद्राजनं देवतासु प्रोतम्
transliteration: agnirhiṃkāro vāyuḥ prastāva āditya udgītho nakṣatrāṇi pratihāraścandramā nidhanametadrājanaṃ devatāsu protam
translation: Fire is the hiṃkāra, air is the prastāva, the sun is the udgītha, the stars are the pratihāra, and the moon is the nidhana . This Sāma known as Rājana is rooted in the gods and goddesses.
word_meaning: Agniḥ hiṃkāraḥ, fire is the hiṃkāra; vāyuḥ prastāvaḥ, air is the prastāva; ādityaḥ udgīthaḥ, the sun is the udgītha; nakṣatrāṇi pratihāraḥ, the stars are the pratihāra; candramāḥ nidhanam, the moon is the nidhana; etat rājanam, this [Sāma called] Rājana; devatāsu protam, is rooted in the gods and goddesses.
commentary: In the previous section the Sāma was worshipped in the parts of the body. Now it is being worshipped in the deities—that is, in the forces of nature. Fire is the first among the forces of nature, so it is the hiṃkāra. Next to the hiṃkāra is the prastāva. Air is called the prastāva because it comes next after fire, and it is also infinite. The sun is the udgītha, for just as the udgītha is the best among the Sāma songs, so also the sun is the best among the forces of nature. The stars lie scattered, and as we locate them it seems that we are ‘collecting’ ( pratihāra ) them. That is why the stars are said to be the pratihāra. The moon is said to be the nidhana, because active people go to Candraloka, the world of the moon, after death. The Sāma called Rājana is rooted in the gods and goddesses, for the deities are by nature luminous ( rājana ).
contextual_topics: Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
claim_candidates: The identification of fire with hiṃkāra implies that the primal sound of creation is embodied in the element fire
Air being termed prastāva suggests that the principle of expansion or offering is represented by the pervasive nature of air
The sun's designation as udgītha indicates that the sun is the supreme among natural forces, analogous to the best Sāma song
The moon's association with nidhana links the lunar realm to the destination of active souls after death
The Sāma called Rājana being rooted in the gods because deities are luminous shows that liturgical music reflects the inherent luminosity of divine beings
objection_hooks: The correlation between hiṃkāra and fire may be symbolic rather than ontological, questioning whether the sound truly embodies fire
Interpreting air as prastāva as 'expansion' could be an extrapolation beyond the textual meaning of the term
The claim that the moon is the destination of active souls after death may conflict with other Upanishadic teachings about the afterlife
Asserting that the Sāma's root in deities proves music reflects divine luminosity might be a rhetorical flourish lacking doctrinal support

sanskrit: स य एवमेतद्राजनं देवतासु प्रोतं वेदैतासामेव देवतानांसलोकतांसर्ष्टितांसायुज्यं गच्छति सर्वमायुरेति ज्योग्जीवति महान्प्रजया पशुभिर्भवति महान्कीर्त्या ब्राह्मणान्न निन्देत्तद्व्रतम्
transliteration: sa ya evametadrājanaṃ devatāsu protaṃ vedaitāsāmeva devatānāṃsalokatāṃsarṣṭitāṃsāyujyaṃ gacchati sarvamāyureti jyogjīvati mahānprajayā paśubhirbhavati mahānkīrtyā brāhmaṇānna nindettadvratam
translation: He who knows that the Sāma known as Rājana is established in the gods and goddesses shares the same worlds with these gods and goddesses, has the same rights and privileges with them, or has the same form. He also has a long and brilliant life. And he becomes great by virtue of his children and his animal wealth, and also by virtue of his great deeds. His vow is that he will never speak ill of the brāhmins.
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ evam etat rājanam devatāsu protam veda, he who knows that this Sāma known as Rājana is established in the gods and goddesses [such as Agni (fire), Vāyu (air), etc.]; etāsām eva devatānām salokatām gacchati, he shares with those gods and goddesses the same worlds; sārṣṭitām, the same rights and privileges; [ vā ] sāyujyam, [or] the same form; sarvam āyuḥ eti, he lives the full span of his life; jyok jīvati, he has a brilliant life; mahān prajayā paśubhiḥ bhavati, he becomes great by virtue of his children and also his animal wealth; mahān kīrtyā, he is great by his great deeds; brāhmaṇān na nindet tat vratam, it is his vow that he will not speak ill of the brāhmins.
commentary: What does a person gain from worshipping the Sāma in such a way? He gets the right to live with the gods and goddesses in the same world, or to share the same rights and privileges with them, or to have the same form. It is not that he would get all these things. He would get any one of them. The scriptures say that the brāhmins themselves are the gods and goddesses. Obviously then one should not say anything derogatory about the brāhmins.
contextual_topics: Progressive Worship of Brahman up to the Universal Self
Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Worship of the Sāma (Rājana) grants the devotee the same status as the gods, including shared worlds, rights, or form
The benefits of such worship are exclusive; the devotee obtains only one of the possible divine privileges
The Brahmins are equated with gods and goddesses, making disrespect toward them equivalent to disrespect toward the divine
A vow to never speak ill of Brahmins is an essential ethical component of the worship of Sāma
objection_hooks: How can a mortal attain the same form as a deity merely through worship, given the ontological gap between human and divine?
If the benefits are exclusive, what determines which specific privilege the devotee receives, and is this selection arbitrary?
The equation of Brahmins with deities may reflect a social hierarchy rather than an ontological truth; does the text provide justification beyond scriptural assertion?
Is the injunction to never speak ill of Brahmins intended as a universal moral law or only as a contextual requirement of this particular ritual practice?

sanskrit: त्रयी विद्या हिंकारस्त्रय इमे लोकाः स प्रस्तावोऽग्निर्वायुरादित्यः स उद्गीथो नक्षत्राणि वयांसि मरीचयः स प्रतिहारः सर्पा गन्धर्वाः पितरस्तन्निधनमेतत्साम सर्वस्मिन्प्रोतम्
transliteration: trayī vidyā hiṃkārastraya ime lokāḥ sa prastāvo'gnirvāyurādityaḥ sa udgītho nakṣatrāṇi vayāṃsi marīcayaḥ sa pratihāraḥ sarpā gandharvāḥ pitarastannidhanametatsāma sarvasminprotam
translation: The three vidyās [the Ṛk, the Yajuḥ, and the Sāma ] are together the hiṃkāra; these three worlds [the earth, the space between the earth and heaven, and heaven] are together the prastāva; fire, air, and the sun are together the udgītha; the stars, the birds, and the rays are together the pratihāra; serpents, gandharvas, and the ancestors are together the nidhana . This Sāma resides in everything.
word_meaning: Trayī vidyā hiṃkāraḥ, the three Vedas [the Ṛk, the Yajuḥ, and the Sāma] are the hiṃkāra; trayaḥ ime lokāḥ, these three worlds [bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ]; saḥ prastāvaḥ, [together] that is the prastāva; agniḥ vāyuḥ ādityaḥ, fire, air, and the sun; saḥ udgīthaḥ, [together] that is the udgītha; nakṣatrāṇi vayāṃsi marīcayaḥ, the stars, the birds, and the rays; saḥ pratihāraḥ, [together] that is the pratihāra; sarpaḥ gandharvāḥ pitaraḥ, serpents, gandharvas [celestial musicians ], and the ancestors; tat nidhanam, [together] that is the nidhana; etat sāma sarvasmin protam, this Sāma rests in everything.
commentary: According to the scriptures the Ṛg Veda comes from fire, the Yajur Veda comes from air, and the Sāma Veda comes from the sun. In the previous section the worship of the Sāma as fire, air, etc., was discussed. Now the worship of the Sāma as the three Vedas is taken up. Knowledge of the three Vedas may be regarded as the hiṃkāra, for you have to use the hiṃkāra before you start doing any worship. After the hiṃkāra comes the prastāva. Similarly, after the three Vedas come the three worlds, so they are said to be the prastāva. Fire, air, and the sun are like the udgītha, for among all things they are of a higher order. The stars, the birds, and the rays come and go, so they are like the pratihāra. The serpents, the gandharvas, and The word Sāma does not refer to any specific Sāma. It refers to anything bearing that name. The word is meant according to the context, just as oblations are offered according to the deities for whom they are meant.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
Being as the Source of All
claim_candidates: The three Vedas collectively constitute the foundational knowledge required for all ritual worship
The three worlds are symbolically identified with the initial stage of worship called prastāva
Fire, air, and the sun represent the higher order of worship and thus embody the supreme aspect of the divine
The Sāma, as a principle, pervades all categories of existence, indicating an immanent universal self
objection_hooks: One might question whether the three Vedas alone constitute hiṃkāra, since hiṃkāra is traditionally an invocatory mantra rather than mere knowledge
Identifying fire, air, and the sun as the highest order could be challenged as overlooking other elemental forces such as water or earth
Equating Sāma with the pervasiveness of everything may conflate a specific Vedic text with the universal Brahman, leading to a category error
Equating the three worlds with prastāva might be seen as metaphorical and lacking empirical basis, thus questionable as a doctrinal statement

sanskrit: स य एवमेतत्साम सर्वस्मिन्प्रोतं वेद सर्वं ह भवति
transliteration: sa ya evametatsāma sarvasminprotaṃ veda sarvaṃ ha bhavati
translation: He who knows that this Sāma is in everything becomes one with everything [or, becomes the Lord of everything].
word_meaning: Saḥ yaḥ evam etat sāma sarvasmin protam veda, he who knows that this Sāma resides in everything; sarvam ha bhavati, he becomes everything.
commentary: This is an example of how far the benefit of the knowledge of the Sāma can extend: If you know that the Sāma is everywhere and in everything, you become the supreme Lord of everything.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
Being as the Source of All
claim_candidates: Knowing that the sacred hymn pervades all reality implies that the ultimate reality is immanent in every phenomenon
Realization of the omnipresence of Sāma leads to the dissolution of individual distinction, resulting in the self becoming identical with the totality
The verse suggests that experiential knowledge of the universal presence of Sāma is sufficient for attaining supreme lordship without external ritual
The claim that the knowledge of Sāma's ubiquity transforms the knower into the lord of everything presupposes that consciousness can merge with Brahman through intellectual insight alone
The teaching implies that the ultimate goal is not merely liberation but the attainment of cosmic sovereignty through self‑realization
objection_hooks: How can mere intellectual knowledge of a hymn's pervasiveness effect ontological transformation
The claim that the knower becomes the lord of everything seems to conflate metaphorical authority with literal cosmic power
If the Sāma is present in everything, does that not make the distinction between knower and known irrelevant, raising ontological confusion
The verse may be hyperbolic; does it prescribe a universal principle or a poetic exaggeration

sanskrit: तदेष श्लोको यानि पञ्चधा त्रीणी त्रीणि तेभ्यो न ज्यायः परमन्यदस्ति
transliteration: tadeṣa śloko yāni pañcadhā trīṇī trīṇi tebhyo na jyāyaḥ paramanyadasti
translation: Here is a verse in this connection: There are five parts of Sāma, and each of these is divided into three parts. There is nothing higher than these [fifteen forms of Sāma].
word_meaning: Tat eṣaḥ ślokaḥ, here is a verse on the subject; yāni pañcadhā, that [Sāma] which is divided into five parts [hiṃkāra, prastāva, udgītha, pratihāra, and nidhana ]; trīṇi trīṇi, each again divided into three parts [such as hiṃkāra representing the three Vedas ]; tebhyaḥ jyāyaḥ param anyat na asti, there is nothing higher than these.
commentary: So long we have discussed the five forms of the Sāma: hiṃkāra, prastāva, udgītha, pratihāra, and nidhana. In the present verse the Upaniṣad says that each of these five can be divided further into three: hiṃkāra as the Ṛk, the Yajuḥ, and the Sāma; prastāva as the earth, the intermediate space (between the earth and heaven), and heaven; udgītha as fire, air, and the sun; pratihāra as the stars, the birds, and the rays; and nidhana as the snakes, the celestial musicians, and the ancestors. It is Sāma which is manifest in all of these fifteen
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The fifteen forms of Sāma constitute the highest attainable spiritual expression
Each of the five categories of Sāma corresponds to a triadic division that maps onto fundamental elements of the cosmos
The structure of Sāma reflects a microcosmic representation of the universal order
The Sāma is manifest in all fifteen divisions, indicating its pervasive presence
The classification of Sāma into five and three parts suggests an inherent hierarchical order in Vedic knowledge
objection_hooks: How can a liturgical classification be considered higher than other spiritual practices
The correspondence between Sāma divisions and cosmic elements may be symbolic rather than ontological
The assertion that Sāma is manifest in all fifteen forms does not necessarily imply a universal self
The hierarchical ordering may reflect cultural preferences rather than an intrinsic metaphysical hierarchy

sanskrit: यस्तद्वेद स वेद सर्वं सर्वा दिशो बलिमस्मै हरन्ति सर्वमस्मीत्युपासित तद्व्रतं तद्व्रतम्
transliteration: yastadveda sa veda sarvaṃ sarvā diśo balimasmai haranti sarvamasmītyupāsita tadvrataṃ tadvratam
translation: He who knows Sāma knows everything, and gifts come to him from all quarters. His vow will be to constantly say to himself, ‘I am one with all’.
word_meaning: Yaḥ tat veda, he who knows that [Sāma]; saḥ veda sarvam, he knows all; sarvāḥ diśaḥ, all the quarters; balim, gifts; asmai, for him; haranti, bring; sarvam asmi, I am all; iti upāsīta, this is how he will meditate; tat vratam tat vratam, this is his vow, this is his vow.
commentary: Sāma is the inmost being of all, and he who knows it as such becomes like Sāma—that is, he becomes the inmost being of all, and he knows everything. People come from everywhere with gifts to show him their respect. ‘I am Sāma, the inmost being of all’—this is how Sāma is to be worshipped. One should constantly repeat this to oneself. In fact, it should be treated as a vow.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: Knowing Sāma (the inmost being) confers knowledge of all phenomena
The realization "I am all" functions as a self‑vow that transforms the practitioner into the universal self
External gifts are drawn to one who has realized the inmost being, indicating societal recognition of spiritual attainment
Repetition of the identity statement constitutes a valid meditative practice leading to unity with Brahman
The inmost being (Sāma) is identical with the individual self, implying non‑duality
objection_hooks: How can knowledge of an abstract principle guarantee knowledge of all concrete things?
Does the claim that external gifts are attracted to the realized self rely on empirical evidence or is it metaphorical?
Is the self‑identification "I am all" logically coherent, or does it collapse distinction between subject and object?

sanskrit: विनर्दि साम्नो वृणे पशव्यमित्यग्नेरुद्गीथोऽनिरुक्तः प्रजापतेर्निरुक्तः सोमस्य मृदु श्लक्ष्णं वायोः श्लक्ष्णं बलवदिन्द्रस्य क्रौञ्चं बृहस्पतेरपध्वान्तं वरुणस्य तान्सर्वानेवोपसेवेत वारुणं त्वेव वर्जयेत्
transliteration: vinardi sāmno vṛṇe paśavyamityagnerudgītho'niruktaḥ prajāpaterniruktaḥ somasya mṛdu ślakṣṇaṃ vāyoḥ ślakṣṇaṃ balavadindrasya krauñcaṃ bṛhaspaterapadhvāntaṃ varuṇasya tānsarvānevopaseveta vāruṇaṃ tveva varjayet
translation: The vinardi voice for singing the Sāma is good for animals, and Agni, the god of fire, is its presiding deity. I bear this in mind and pray that I may have this voice. The god Prajāpati presides over the udgītha sung in the anirukta [unclear] voice. The one having Soma as its presiding deity is nirukta [clear]. That of Vāyu, the god of air, is soft and pleasant, and Indra ’s is strong. That which has Bṛhaspati as its presiding deity is like the voice of the krauñca bird, and that of Varuṇa is like the sound of a broken metal pot. Cultivate all of these, but avoid the one of Varuṇa.
word_meaning: Vinardi, the voice called vinardi, which is deep, like that of a bull; sāmnaḥ, for [singing] the Sāma; vṛṇe iti, I pray for; paśavyam, good for animals; agneḥ, of the god of fire; udgītha aniruktaḥ, the udgītha sung in the anirukta voice, which is not very distinct; prajāpateḥ, of Prajāpati, the Lord of all; niruktaḥ, the voice called nirukta, which is clear; somasya, of the god Soma; mṛdu ślakṣṇam, the voice called ślakṣṇa that is soft and soothing; vāyoḥ, of the god Vāyu, air; ślakṣṇam balavat, the voice called ślakṣṇa that is soothing yet powerful; indrasya, of Indra; krauñcam, the voice called krauñca, which is like that of the krauñca bird; bṛhaspateḥ, of Bṛhaspati; apadhvāntam, the voice called apadhvānta, which sounds like a broken metal pot; varuṇasya, of the god Varuṇa; tān sarvān era upaseveta, practise on all of them; tu eva vāruṇam, except that of Varuṇa; varjayet, one should avoid.
commentary: When you sing the udgītha, be careful that you sing it in the right voice. The voice is important because it determines the benefit you derive from your singing. For instance, there is a type of voice that sounds like that of a bull. Agni, fire, is the presiding deity of this voice. If you sing the udgītha in this type of voice, it means you are singing for the good of the animals and you are also praying that you may have that kind of voice. Similarly, there is a type of voice called anirukta, which has Prajāpati as its presiding deity. Prajāpati, the Lord of all beings, has no form of his own. Similarly, he does not have a distinct voice. This is why it is called anirukta, indistinct. The voice of Soma, the moon, is nirukta, clear; that of Indra is powerful; and that of Bṛhaspati sounds like a krauñca, a bird similar to a crane. Varuṇa’s voice is the worst. It is like the sound of a broken brass vessel. All these voices can be used except that of Varuṇa.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
The Sacred Syllable Om
claim_candidates: The quality of the vocal tone used in singing the udgītha determines the spiritual benefit derived from the ritual
Each classified voice type is linked to a specific deity, indicating that the deity’s characteristic is expressed through that voice
The voice associated with Varuṇa is deemed detrimental and should be avoided in ritual singing
The voice termed nirukta, described as clear, is connected with Soma, suggesting a correspondence between vocal clarity and the moon deity’s nature
objection_hooks: How can a mere vocal timbre influence spiritual outcomes when ritual efficacy is traditionally based on intention rather than acoustic qualities
The association of deities with voice types may be symbolic rather than literal, calling into question whether deity attributes are truly reflected in the voice
Varuṇa governs water and cosmic order; labeling its voice as harmful may reflect cultural bias rather than an inherent negative quality
The link between a clear voice (nirukta) and Soma could be arbitrary; why should vocal clarity correspond to the nature of the moon deity

sanskrit: अमृतत्वं देवेभ्य आगायानीत्यागायेत्स्वधां पितृभ्य आशां मनुष्येभ्यस्तृणोदकं पशुभ्यः स्वर्गं लोकं यजमानायान्नमात्मन आगायानीत्येतानि मनसा ध्यायन्नप्रमत्तः स्तुवीत
transliteration: amṛtatvaṃ devebhya āgāyānītyāgāyetsvadhāṃ pitṛbhya āśāṃ manuṣyebhyastṛṇodakaṃ paśubhyaḥ svargaṃ lokaṃ yajamānāyānnamātmana āgāyānītyetāni manasā dhyāyannapramattaḥ stuvīta
translation: One should sing with the resolve: ‘By singing I will get immortality for the gods and goddesses, food offerings for the ancestors, hope for humanity, food and water for the animals, heaven for those who perform sacrifices, and food for myself. All this I will get by singing.’ Thinking thus, one should sing without raising the voice too much [or, without being too excited].
word_meaning: Āgāyet, one should sing [with the resolve]; amṛtatvam devebhyaḥ āgāyāni iti, I will get immortality for the gods and goddesses by singing; svadhām, offerings; pitṛbhyaḥ, for the ancestors; āśām manuṣyebhyaḥ, hope for humanity; tṛṇodakam paśubhyaḥ, food and water for the animals; svargam lokam, heavenly worlds; yajamānāya, for those who perform sacrifices; annam ātmane, food for myself; āgāyāni iti, I shall win by singing thus; etāni, all these; manasā dhyāyan, thinking mentally; apramattaḥ, without raising the voice too much; stuvīta, one should sing.
commentary: When you sing the Sāma, you should keep in mind the things you are singing for—such as immortality for the gods and goddesses, etc. But you must also take care that when you sing, your pronunciation and accents are correct, and that you do not miss any syllables.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Singing with the resolve that it yields benefits is a valid means to obtain those benefits
The benefits listed are attainable through the act of singing alone, without additional ritual actions
The proper execution of singing requires mental focus and restraint, implying that the quality of intention affects the efficacy of the practice
The act of singing serves as a substitute for material offerings to gods, ancestors, and beings, thereby replacing traditional sacrificial rites
The verse includes personal benefit alongside altruistic benefits, indicating that self‑interest is acceptable within this spiritual practice
objection_hooks: Is mere intention sufficient to guarantee material benefits, or does it rely on divine grace beyond human control
Does the verse truly eliminate the need for external ritual, or is singing merely an adjunct to traditional sacrifice
The instruction to not raise the voice may be about decorum, not about efficacy; does restraint truly affect the outcome
Including self‑benefit may contradict the principle of selflessness in Vedic ethics; is this endorsement of selfish motive

sanskrit: सर्वे स्वरा इन्द्रस्यात्मानः सर्व ऊष्माणः प्रजापतेरात्मानः सर्वे स्पर्शा मृत्योरात्मानस्तं यदि स्वरेषूपालभेतेन्द्रंशरणं प्रपन्नोऽभूवं स त्वा प्रति वक्ष्यतीत्येनं ब्रूयात्
transliteration: sarve svarā indrasyātmānaḥ sarva ūṣmāṇaḥ prajāpaterātmānaḥ sarve sparśā mṛtyorātmānastaṃ yadi svareṣūpālabhetendraṃśaraṇaṃ prapanno'bhūvaṃ sa tvā prati vakṣyatītyenaṃ brūyāt
translation: All the vowels are like Indra ’s body with its various parts. The sibilants [śa, ṣa, etc.] are like Prajāpati ’s body with its various parts. The consonants, starting with ka, are the body and limbs of Death. If someone finds fault with the way the udgātā pronounces the vowels, he may say to that person: ‘As I began singing, I took refuge in Indra [i.e., I sought Indra’s blessings]. Ask him and he will give you the right answer [to your criticism].’
word_meaning: Sarve svarāḥ, all the vowels; indrasya ātmānaḥ, are like the body [with its limbs] of Indra; sarve ūṣmāṇaḥ, all the sibilants; prajāpateḥ ātmānaḥ, are like the body [with its limbs] of Prajāpati; sarve sparśāḥ, all the consonants, starting with ka; mṛtyoḥ ātmānaḥ, are like the body [with all its limbs] of Death; yadi upālabheta, if anyone criticizes; tam, him [the udgātā, who is singing the Sāma ]; svareṣu, regarding his pronunciation of the vowels; indram śaraṇam prapannaḥ abhūvam, [the udgātā will then say: ] I took refuge in Indra [when I started singing the vowels]; saḥ, he [Indra]; tvā prativakṣyati iti, will give you the right reply; enam brūyāt, say to him.
commentary: The vowels are said to be Indra’s body, for when you start doing something, including even a recitation, you have to feel strong enough to do the job fully and correctly. And in order that you may feel that you have the requisite strength, you pray for Indra’s blessings, and you feel that he is transmitting his strength to you. You feel that the vowels you are using are his body, the sibilants are the body of Prajāpati, and the consonants are the body of Death. Then if anyone criticizes your pronunciation of the vowels, you can tell him to ask Indra for the reason
contextual_topics: The Sacred Syllable Om
claim_candidates: The classification of vowels, sibilants and consonants as bodies of specific deities implies that sound is a manifestation of divine reality
Seeking refuge in Indra at the start of a vocal performance reflects a belief that divine support is necessary for correct articulation of sacred sounds
The identification of consonants with the body of Death suggests that certain sounds embody destructive or limiting aspects of existence
The verse proposes that criticism of one’s pronunciation can be resolved by invoking divine authority rather than through rational argument
objection_hooks: The equation of phonetic categories with divine bodies may be metaphorical and does not entail ontological identity, so the claim overstates the verse’s implication
The association of consonants with Death could be culturally arbitrary; why assign destructive quality to consonants rather than to other sounds
Deferring to divine authority to settle a criticism avoids rational discourse and raises epistemic concerns about the validity of such a resolution
The practice of seeking Indra’s blessings might be a poetic device rather than a literal theological necessity, questioning the claim’s interpretation

sanskrit: अथ यद्येनमूष्मसूपालभेत प्रजापतिंशरणं प्रपन्नोऽभूवं स त्वा प्रति पेक्ष्यतीत्येनं ब्रूयादथ यद्येनं स्पर्शेषूपालभेत मृत्युं शरणं प्रपन्नोऽभूवं स त्वा प्रति धक्ष्यतीत्येनं ब्रूयात्
transliteration: atha yadyenamūṣmasūpālabheta prajāpatiṃśaraṇaṃ prapanno'bhūvaṃ sa tvā prati pekṣyatītyenaṃ brūyādatha yadyenaṃ sparśeṣūpālabheta mṛtyuṃ śaraṇaṃ prapanno'bhūvaṃ sa tvā prati dhakṣyatītyenaṃ brūyāt
translation: Then, if someone finds fault with his pronunciation of the sibilants, the singer will say to him: ‘When I started singing I sought Prajāpati ’s blessings. He will therefore crush you.’ Then, if someone finds fault with his pronunciation of the consonants, the singer will say to him: ‘I sought Death’s protection while singing. He will therefore burn you to ashes’.
word_meaning: Atha, then; yadi enam ūṣmasu upālabheta, if a person criticizes him for his pronunciation of the sibilants; prajāpatim śaraṇam prapanṇaḥ abhūvam, I took refuge in Prajāpati [when I started singing]; saḥ, he [Prajāpati]; tvā pratipekṣati iti, will crush you; enam brūyāt, he will say to him; atha, then; yadi enam sparśeṣu upālabheta, if someone criticizes him for his pronunciation of the consonants; mṛtyum śaraṇam prapannaḥ abhūvam, I took refuge in Death [when I started singing]; saḥ, he [Death]; tvā pratidhakṣyati iti, will burn you to ashes; enam brūyāt, he will say to him.
commentary: If you are reciting a hymn, seek Prajāpati’s protection concerning the sibilants. Then, even if you err, he will protect you. Similarly, you should seek Death’s protection concerning the consonants. He will protect you from harm for any mistakes you might make. In fact, those who find fault with you will themselves be punished, for by criticizing your singing, they are insulting Prajāpati or Death.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: Seeking Prajapati's protection for correct pronunciation of sibilants guarantees divine retribution against critics
Invoking Death's protection for consonant pronunciation makes Death act as a guardian of the singer's performance
The singer's reliance on divine patrons indicates that devotional refuge supersedes the need for perfect pronunciation
Criticizing a singer's pronunciation is equivalent to insulting the divine entities invoked, thus meriting punishment
objection_hooks: How can Death, a destructive force, be a protector of a singer's artistic expression
Does invoking divine protection truly ensure safety, or is it merely a superstition without logical basis
The emphasis on external divine aid seems to diminish the value of personal effort in mastering pronunciation
The punishment of critics may be metaphorical; is it appropriate to infer literal divine retribution

sanskrit: सर्वे स्वरा घोषवन्तो बलवन्तो वक्तव्या इन्द्रे बलं ददानीति सर्व ऊष्माणोऽग्रस्ता अनिरस्ता विवृता वक्तव्याः प्रजापतेरात्मानं परिददानीति सर्वे स्पर्शा लेशेनानभिनिहिता वक्तव्या मृत्योरात्मानं परिहराणीति
transliteration: sarve svarā ghoṣavanto balavanto vaktavyā indre balaṃ dadānīti sarva ūṣmāṇo'grastā anirastā vivṛtā vaktavyāḥ prajāpaterātmānaṃ paridadānīti sarve sparśā leśenānabhinihitā vaktavyā mṛtyorātmānaṃ pariharāṇīti
translation: Each vowel should be articulated clearly and powerfully, [and while doing so, you should think, ] ‘I will give some of my strength to Indra .’ The sibilants also should be uttered fully and distinctly, without sounding as if you are swallowing part of them or spitting them out.
