transliteration: na ha vā asmā udeti na nimlocati sakṛddivā haivāsmai bhavati ya etāmevaṃ brahmopaniṣadaṃ veda
translation: For him who knows the secret teachings of Brahman there is no sunrise or sunset [or day or night]. For him there is always day [i.e., light].
word_meaning: Na, not; ha vai asmai, so far as he is concerned; udeti, does [the sun] rise; na nimlocati, nor does it set; asmai, for him; sakṛt divā ha eva bhavati, there is always day [i.e., light]; yaḥ, he who; etām, this; evam, in this way; brahmopaniṣadam, the secret teachings about Brahman; veda, knows.
commentary: Earlier it was described how Brahman manifests itself in various forms—as a crossbeam, a honeycomb, etc., or as various gods enjoying various nectars. If you understand the underlying meaning of such manifestations, you then attain the knowledge of Brahman. To you then there is no day or night. You are like the sun—self-luminous. You are, in fact, one with Brahman—always the same, eternal, infinite.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Knowledge of the secret teachings of Brahman eliminates the experience of temporal cycles such as sunrise and sunset
The knower of Brahman becomes self‑luminous like the sun, independent of external illumination
Attaining knowledge of Brahman leads to the realization that the individual self is identical with the infinite Brahman
The state of always‑day for the knower implies that liberation transcends the dualities of day and night
objection_hooks: If sunrise and sunset are said to cease for the knower, how does this account for the observable changes in the external world
The claim that the knower becomes self‑luminous may be metaphorical; can it be taken as a literal ontological transformation
Equating the individual self with infinite Brahman might ignore the empirical distinction between subject and object, raising an ontological confusion

sanskrit: तद्धैतद्ब्रह्मा प्रजापतय उवाच प्रजापतिर्मनवे मनुः प्रजाभ्यस्तद्धैतदुद्दालकायारुणये ज्येष्ठाय पुत्राय पिता ब्रह्म प्रोवाच
transliteration: taddhaitadbrahmā prajāpataya uvāca prajāpatirmanave manuḥ prajābhyastaddhaitaduddālakāyāruṇaye jyeṣṭhāya putrāya pitā brahma provāca
translation: First, Brahmā taught this instruction on honey to Prajāpati . Then Prajāpati taught it to Manu, and Manu taught it to his children. The father Aruṇa then taught this knowledge of Brahman to his eldest son Uddālaka Āruṇi .
word_meaning: Tat ha etat, that [i.e., the teaching on honey]; brahmā prajāpataya uvāca, Brahmā [first] taught to Prajāpati; prajāpatiḥ manave, Prajāpati [taught it] to Manu; manuḥ prajābhyaḥ, Manu [taught it] to his children; tat ha etat, that; brahma, [knowledge of] Brahman; pitā provāca, the father [Aruṇa] taught; jyeṣṭhāya putrāya uddālakāya āruṇaye, to his eldest son Uddālaka Āruṇi.
commentary: Starting from Brahmā, this knowledge has passed from generation to generation. The mention of this is only to emphasize its importance. This instruction on honey is nothing but Brahma- vidyā, the knowledge of Brahman. It is the secret of how to attain Brahman.
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The lineage transmission of Brahman knowledge confers its authority
The instruction on honey functions as a metaphor for the secret method of attaining Brahman
Knowledge of Brahman is presented as essential instruction from the creator deity to humanity
The hierarchical teaching sequence indicates that spiritual knowledge requires proper generational transmission
Familial instruction as exemplified by Aruṇa teaching Uddālaka validates family as a conduit for spiritual teaching
objection_hooks: The claim that the honey instruction is metaphorical may be challenged by interpreting it as literal guidance on honey production
Asserting that lineage confers legitimacy could be disputed on the basis that personal realization, not ancestry, determines authority
The idea that spiritual knowledge must be hierarchical conflicts with Advaita’s emphasis on direct, non‑mediated insight

sanskrit: इदं वाव तज्ज्येष्ठाय पुत्राय पिता ब्रह्म प्रब्रूयात्प्रणाय्याय वान्तेवासिने
transliteration: idaṃ vāva tajjyeṣṭhāya putrāya pitā brahma prabrūyātpraṇāyyāya vāntevāsine
translation: This knowledge of Brahman a father will pass on to his eldest son or to a competent resident student.
word_meaning: Tat vāva idam brahma, this knowledge of Brahman [previously mentioned as passing from teacher to student]; pitā jyeṣṭhāya putrāya, the father to his eldest son; vā, or; praṇāyyāya, a fit; antevāsine, resident student; prabrūyāt, will teach [or, pass on].
commentary: The knowledge of Brahman is the highest gift a person can confer on another. A father who has this knowledge can give it to his eldest son, or a competent teacher can pass it on to a competent student living with him.
claim_candidates: The transmission of Brahman knowledge from father to eldest son is a legitimate means of spiritual inheritance.
A competent resident student is an appropriate recipient of Brahman knowledge from a teacher.
Knowledge of Brahman constitutes the highest possible gift one can give.
Eligibility to receive Brahman knowledge depends on the recipient's competence or suitability.
Those who possess Brahman knowledge have a duty to teach it.
objection_hooks: How is "eldest son" defined as inherently more qualified than other children?
What criteria determine a "competent resident student", and can this be objectively assessed?
Claiming knowledge of Brahman as the highest gift may overlook other virtues such as compassion; is this hierarchy justified?
If knowledge of Brahman is the highest gift, why is it limited to certain recipients rather than being universally accessible?

sanskrit: नान्यस्मै कस्मैचन यद्यप्यस्मा इमामद्भिः परिगृहीतां धनस्य पूर्णां दद्यादेतदेव ततो भूय इत्येतदेव ततो भूय इति
transliteration: nānyasmai kasmaicana yadyapyasmā imāmadbhiḥ parigṛhītāṃ dhanasya pūrṇāṃ dadyādetadeva tato bhūya ityetadeva tato bhūya iti
translation: This should never be taught to anyone else, even if one is tempted with the whole world full of riches and surrounded by water. For this knowledge is more precious than that. This knowledge is surely more precious than that.
word_meaning: Na anyasmai kasmaicana, to nobody else; yadi api asmai, even if to him [to the teacher]; imām, this [world]; adbhiḥ parigṛhītām, surrounded by water; dhanasya pūrṇām, full of gold; dadyāt, gives; etat, this [instruction on honey]; eva tataḥ bhūyaḥ. iti, is more precious than that [the repetition is for emphasis].
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: The transmission of sacred knowledge should be restricted to the teacher alone, regardless of material temptation
Spiritual knowledge holds greater value than any amount of worldly wealth
The secrecy of this instruction implies its transformative power surpasses material abundance
True wealth is identified with the knowledge itself rather than external riches
objection_hooks: How can one be certain that the knowledge is intrinsically more valuable than material wealth without empirical verification
The injunction against sharing knowledge may conflict with the principle of disseminating spiritual truth for the benefit of all
The claim that secrecy indicates transformative power assumes that hidden knowledge is inherently superior, which may be a rhetorical device rather than a logical necessity

sanskrit: गायत्री वा ईदं सर्वं भूतं यदिदं किं च वाग्वै गायत्री वाग्वा इदं सर्वं भूतं गायति च त्रायते च
transliteration: gāyatrī vā īdaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ yadidaṃ kiṃ ca vāgvai gāyatrī vāgvā idaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ gāyati ca trāyate ca
translation: All that exists in this world, whatever there is, is gāyatrī . It is the word that is gāyatrī, for the word gives names to all things and it also tells them not to fear.
word_meaning: Gāyatrī vai idam sarvam bhūtam, all these beings are gāyatrī; yat idam kiñca, whatever is there; vāk vai gāyatrī, the word is gāyatrī; vāk vai idam sarvam bhūtam gāyati ca, it is vāk that gives names [or sings] to all things; trāyate ca, and also gives protection.
commentary: Here the importance of the gāyatrī is Being emphasized. True, the gāyatrī is poetry, but it is that poetry which leads to Brahman . This gāyatrī is also called vāk, word, because it is vāk which identifies everything that exists. Vāk gives everything a name and thereby gives it a status. The word gāyatrī means gāyati ca trāyate ca —that which gives names (or sings) to things and also gives them protection. It also means gāyantam trāyate —that is, he who repeats the gāyatrī is saved. ( Ga means singing, and tra means saving or protecting.)
contextual_topics: Being as the Source of All
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The Gāyatrī hymn is identical to the ultimate reality that pervades all beings
The word (vāk) functions as the principle that names and thereby confers existence to all things
Recitation of the Gāyatrī provides protection to those who hear or repeat it
Understanding the Gāyatrī as word leads one toward realization of Brahman
objection_hooks: How can a hymn be equated with the totality of existence?
Does naming something truly confer its existence, or merely describe it?
Is the protection offered by the hymn dependent on belief, making it subjective?
Can the Gāyatrī be said to lead to Brahman for all, given varied interpretations?

sanskrit: या वै सा गायत्रीयं वाव सा येयं पृथिव्यस्यां हीदं सर्वं भूतं प्रतिष्ठितमेतामेव नातिशीयते
transliteration: yā vai sā gāyatrīyaṃ vāva sā yeyaṃ pṛthivyasyāṃ hīdaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ pratiṣṭhitametāmeva nātiśīyate
translation: That which is this gāyatrī is that which is this earth. For all things [moving or unmoving] are attached to this earth and cannot get away from it.
word_meaning: Yā vai sā gāyatrī, that which is this gāyatrī; iyam vāva sā, it is that; yā iyam pṛthivī, which is this earth; hi, for; asyām, to this [earth]; sarvam bhūtam, all things [moving or unmoving]; pratiṣṭhitam, are attached; etām eva na atiśīyate, cannot get away from it.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle
claim_candidates: The Gayatri mantra is ontologically identical to the earth
All beings, whether animate or inanimate, are permanently affixed to the earth
The earth serves as the sole foundation upon which all existence is established
Because nothing can depart from the earth, liberation must be realized within the earthly realm rather than by escaping it
objection_hooks: If the Gayatri is identical to the earth, how can it be recited as a transcendent sound that purifies the mind
The assertion that nothing can get away from the earth conflicts with Upanishadic teachings of the soul's migration beyond the physical world
Equating a sacred mantra with a material element may diminish its spiritual potency and contradict the notion of Brahman as beyond matter
Claiming the earth as the sole foundation ignores other cosmic principles described in the Upanishads such as the void underlying all

sanskrit: या वै सा पृथिवीयं वाव सा यदिदमस्मिन्पुरुषे शरीरमस्मिन्हीमे प्राणाः प्रतिष्ठिता एतदेव नातिशीयन्ते
transliteration: yā vai sā pṛthivīyaṃ vāva sā yadidamasminpuruṣe śarīramasminhīme prāṇāḥ pratiṣṭhitā etadeva nātiśīyante
translation: That which is this earth is this human body, because all the prāṇas are based in this body and cannot exist independent of it.
word_meaning: Yā vai sā pṛthivī, that which [has earlier been referred to as] this earth; iyam vāva sā, it is that; yat idam asmin puruṣe śarīram, the body which is associated with a human being; hi, because; asmin, on this [body]; ime prāṇāḥ, these prāṇas [i.e., prāṇa, apāna, etc., and also the five elements— ākāśa, vāyu, etc.]; pratiṣṭhitāḥ, are based; etat eva na atiśīyante, they cannot go beyond this [body—i.e., they cannot exist independent of this body].
commentary: The earth is the gāyatrī and this gāyatrī is also the human body because the human body is born of the earth. How is the human body borm of the earth? This body is made up of the same elements (space, air, fire, etc.) that the earth is. The five prāṇas (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna ) are also known as elements, and they rest on this body. The body is therefore the gāyatrī like the earth. It is the gāyatrī because the prāṇas cannot exist without the body.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The human body is ontologically identical to the earth because they share the same elemental composition
All five prāṇas are dependent on the physical body and cannot exist independently of it
The identification of the body with the earth implies that the microcosm reflects the macrocosm
The prāṇas are confined to the body, indicating that the body is the necessary locus for vital forces
objection_hooks: If the body and earth are identical, how does the body undergo change while the earth appears relatively stable
The claim that prāṇas cannot exist independently may be challenged by scriptural references to disembodied souls or deities
Equating microcosm and macrocosm might overlook qualitative differences between human consciousness and planetary processes

sanskrit: यद्वै तत्पुरुषे शरीरमिदं वाव तद्यदिदमस्मिन्नन्तः पुरुषे हृदयमस्मिन्हीमे प्राणाः प्रतिष्ठिता एतदेव नातिशीयन्ते
transliteration: yadvai tatpuruṣe śarīramidaṃ vāva tadyadidamasminnantaḥ puruṣe hṛdayamasminhīme prāṇāḥ pratiṣṭhitā etadeva nātiśīyante
translation: That which is in this human body is in this human heart, for all these prāṇas are based in this heart and cannot exist independent of it.
word_meaning: Yat vai tat puruṣe śarīram, that which is in this human body; idam vāva tat, it is that; yat idam asmin antaḥ puruṣe hṛdayam, which is in this human heart; hi, because; asmin, in this [heart]; ime prāṇāḥ, these prāṇas [the vital forces]; pratiṣṭhitāḥ, are based; etat eva na atiśīyante, they cannot go beyond this [heart—i.e., they cannot exist independent of this heart].
commentary: The human body has been described as the gāyatrī . But where is that gāyatrī? It is in the heart. In fact, the heart is the gāyatrī. In what sense can the heart be called the gāyatrī? In the sense that all the prāṇas are in the heart and cannot exist separate from it. And since the body is the gāyatrī, the heart is also the gāyatrī.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The heart is the essential locus of all vital forces (prāṇas) in the human being.
The human body functions as a manifestation of the sacred hymn (gāyatrī), with the heart embodying that hymn.
Since prāṇas cannot exist independent of the heart, the heart is the indispensable basis for life.
Identifying the heart as the gāyatrī implies that inner consciousness is the true seat of divine expression.
objection_hooks: How can we assert that prāṇas are confined to the heart when physiological observations locate breath and circulation throughout the body?
Does equating the heart with the gāyatrī risk reducing the cosmic hymn to a mere anatomical organ, thereby limiting its universal significance?
If the heart is the sole basis for prāṇas, what explains the functioning of other organs that also sustain life?
Could the claim that the body is the gāyatrī be metaphorical rather than literal, undermining its doctrinal weight?

sanskrit: सैषा चतुष्पदा षड्विधा गायत्री तदेतदृचाभ्यनूक्तम्
transliteration: saiṣā catuṣpadā ṣaḍvidhā gāyatrī tadetadṛcābhyanūktam
translation: The gāyatrī has four quarters, each being sixfold. This is what is stated in a Ṛk mantra: 10.10.3].
word_meaning: Sā eṣā gāyatrī catuṣpadā, this gāyatrī has four feet [i.e., quarters]; ṣaṣvidhā, each of them sixfold; tat etat ṛcā abhyanūktam, this is what is stated in a Ṛk mantra [ Ṛg Veda
commentary: The gāyatrī is also known as Brahma -gāyatrī. It is one with everything. The Upaniṣad says here that the gāyatrī has four quarters and each quarter has six parts (that is, it
contextual_topics: The Universal Self
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The Gāyatrī mantra is described as having four quarters, each composed of six parts, as explicitly stated in Rig Veda 10.10.3
The Upaniṣadic commentary equates the Gāyatrī with Brahma, asserting that the mantra is one with everything
The enumeration of quarters and sixfold divisions in the Gāyatrī serves to symbolize the comprehensive nature of Brahman
By presenting the Gāyatrī’s structure in a mantra, the text implies that the ultimate reality can be apprehended through symbolic representation
objection_hooks: Does the mere structural description of the Gāyatrī guarantee that it symbolically represents the totality of Brahman, or could it be a poetic device without metaphysical import?
The identification of Gāyatrī with Brahma in the commentary may be metaphorical; does this allow the claim that the mantra is ontologically identical to the ultimate reality?
Is the claim that the sixfold divisions correspond to a comprehensive depiction of Brahman supported by explicit textual evidence, or is it an extrapolation beyond the verse?
Can a mantra’s enumeration be taken as a definitive proof of Brahman's nature, or does it merely reflect ritualistic categorization?

sanskrit: तावानस्य महिमा ततो ज्यायांश्च पूरुषः । पादोऽस्य सर्वा भूतानि त्रिपादस्यामृतं दिवीति
transliteration: tāvānasya mahimā tato jyāyāṃśca pūruṣaḥ | pādo'sya sarvā bhūtāni tripādasyāmṛtaṃ divīti
translation: Its glory is like this. But the glory of the puruṣa [i.e., Brahman, who fills the whole world] is still greater. All creatures constitute one quarter of him. The remaining three quarters are nectar in heaven.
word_meaning: Tāvān, like this; asya mahimā, its glory; tataḥ jyāyān ca puruṣaḥ, that [i.e., the glory] of the puruṣa [i.e., Brahman, who fills the whole world] is still greater; pādaḥ asya sarvā [i.e., sarvāṇi] bhūtāni, all things constitute one foot [or, quarter] of him; tripād asya, [the remaining] three feet [or, quarters] of him; amṛtam divi, are like nectar in heaven.
commentary: Brahman has been described as the gāyatrī, having four feet (or, quarters) and being sixfold. This is just figurative, however. Brahman is Brahman and there is no way of describing it. In reality, it is without name and form, beyond thought and speech. It is the Absolute. Brahman can be conceived as both the cause and the effect. As the cause ( karaṇa ) nothing can be predicated about it; it is nirupādhika, without attributes. As the effect ( kārya ) it is sopādhika, with attributes. Similarly, the gāyatrī is said here to have four quarters and six parts. These are attributes used to help a disciple understand. As the Pañcadaśi says (verse II.58), ‘ Niraṃśe api aṃśam āropya ....’ (that is, parts are superimposed on that which has no parts in order to explain what cannot be described).
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The glory of the puruṣa (Brahman) exceeds the glory of any manifested form.
All created beings together constitute only one quarter of Brahman's total reality.
The remaining three quarters of Brahman are likened to nectar in heaven, indicating a blissful unmanifest aspect.
The description of Brahman with four quarters and six parts is a pedagogical metaphor, not an ontological claim of actual parts.
Brahman as cause is attribute‑less (nirupādhika) while as effect it possesses attributes (sopādhika).
objection_hooks: If Brahman is without parts, how can we meaningfully say that creatures make up one quarter of it?
Speaking of Brahman's glory seems contradictory to the claim that the cause aspect of Brahman is attribute‑less.
Using quarters to describe Brahman appears to introduce division, which conflicts with the non‑dual assertion of indivisibility.
Describing three quarters as nectar in heaven may imply a dualistic separation between Brahman and heaven.

sanskrit: यद्वै तद्ब्रह्मेतीदं वाव तद्योयं बहिर्धा पुरुषादाकाशो यो वै स बहिर्धा पुरुषादाकाशः
transliteration: yadvai tadbrahmetīdaṃ vāva tadyoyaṃ bahirdhā puruṣādākāśo yo vai sa bahirdhā puruṣādākāśaḥ
translation: 7-9. That which is Brahman is also the space outside the body. That which is the space outside the body is also the space inside the body. And that which is the space inside the body is also the space within the heart. That treasure within the heart is full and unchanging. He who knows this is always full and not subject to change.
word_meaning: Yat vai tat brahma iti, that which is Brahman; idam vāva tat, it is that; yaḥ, which; ayam, is this; ākāśaḥ, space; bahirdhā puruṣāt, outside the human body; yaḥ vai saḥ ākāśaḥ, that which is the space; bahirdhā puruṣāt, outside the human body; ayam vāva saḥ, it is that; yaḥ ayam ākāśaḥ, which is this space; antaḥ puruṣe, inside the human body; yaḥ vai saḥ antaḥ puruṣe ākāśaḥ, that which is the space inside the human body; ayam vāva saḥ, it is that; yaḥ ayam ākāśaḥ, which is this space; antaḥ hṛdaye, inside the heart; tat etat, it is that; pūrṇam, full; apravarti, unchanging; śriyam, treasure; yaḥ evam veda, he who knows this; pūrṇām apravartinīm labhate, becomes full and is not subject to change.
commentary: Earlier Brahman was described as the gāyatrī with four quarters and also as amṛta, nectar. Here it is described as space. It is the same space which is inside as well as outside the human body, and also within the heart. The Upaniṣad says that this ākāśa in the heart is full and never changes. That is to say, it is free from desire and because of that it is never subject to change. Anyone who knows that ākāśa in the heart as such is himself always full and free from desire.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
claim_candidates: Brahman is identical to the space that pervades both the external universe and the interior of the human body
The innermost space within the heart is a manifestation of Brahman that is full and immutable
Knowing the identity of Brahman with inner space leads to a state of fullness that is free from change and desire
The description of Brahman as space implies that Brahman is non-material and beyond desire, distinguishing it from empirical forms
objection_hooks: If Brahman is equated with physical space, how does it remain non-material and transcendent?
The claim that inner heart space is immutable may conflict with observable physiological changes
Equating knowledge of Brahman with personal fullness could be seen as subjective and not universally verifiable
Identifying Brahman with space might reduce the divine to a mere dimension, undermining its supreme status

sanskrit: तस्य ह वा एतस्य हृदयस्य पञ्च देवसुषयः स योऽस्य प्राङ्सुषिः स प्राणस्तच्चक्षुः स आदित्यस्तदेतत्तेजोऽन्नाद्यमित्युपासीत तेजस्व्यन्नादो भवति य एवं वेद
transliteration: tasya ha vā etasya hṛdayasya pañca devasuṣayaḥ sa yo'sya prāṅsuṣiḥ sa prāṇastaccakṣuḥ sa ādityastadetattejo'nnādyamityupāsīta tejasvyannādo bhavati ya evaṃ veda
translation: In the heart there are five doors guarded by the gods. The door in the east is prāṇa . It is also the eyes, and it is Āditya . Worship this as the source of brightness and food. He who knows this becomes bright and enjoys food.
word_meaning: Tasya ha vai etasya hṛdayasya, of this heart; pañca devasuṣayaḥ, five passages guarded by the gods; saḥ yaḥ, that which; asya prāṅsuṣiḥ, is its eastern passage; saḥ prāṇaḥ, that is prāṇa; tat cakṣuḥ, that is [also] the eye; saḥ ādityaḥ, [and] that is Āditya [the sun]; tat etat, it is that; tejaḥ annādyam iti upāsīta, meditate on as the source of brightness and food; yaḥ evam veda, he who knows this; tejasvī annādaḥ bhavati, becomes bright and an eater of food.
commentary: If you want to enter a house, you must please those who are at the gates. Similarly, if you want to enter heaven, you must worship Brahman as prāṇa. As you do so, you should attribute to prāṇa the qualities of Àditya and annāda —that is, of brightness and strength. If. prāṇa is pleased with you, you have no difficulty attaining heaven.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The worship of prāṇa, identified with Āditya, is presented as a valid means to attain heavenly abode
The heart is described as having five passages guarded by deities, each representing a functional aspect of the self
The eastern passage of the heart corresponds to prāṇa, the eyes, and the sun, indicating a unity of breath, sight, and solar energy
Meditating on prāṇa as the source of brightness and food transforms the practitioner into a luminous being who enjoys sustenance
Knowledge of this correspondence confers brilliance and the ability to partake in food without obstruction
objection_hooks: How can a physiological function like breath be equated with a cosmic deity without conflating metaphor with literal ontology
Does worship of prāṇa alone suffice for attaining heaven, or are additional rites required according to Vedic tradition
The claim that knowledge of the heart's passages leads to brightness and food presupposes a causal link lacking empirical support
If the heart has five doors guarded by gods, why does the verse focus only on the eastern door, neglecting the others

sanskrit: अथ योऽस्य दक्षिणः सुषिः स व्यानस्तच्छ्रोत्रं स चन्द्रमास्तदेतच्छ्रीश्च यशश्चेत्युपासीत श्रीमान्यशस्वी भवति य एवं वेद
transliteration: atha yo'sya dakṣiṇaḥ suṣiḥ sa vyānastacchrotraṃ sa candramāstadetacchrīśca yaśaścetyupāsīta śrīmānyaśasvī bhavati ya evaṃ veda
translation: Next, the southern door of the heart is vyāna . It is also the ears, and it is the moon. Worship it as the source of prosperity and fame. He who knows this becomes prosperous and famous.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yaḥ asya dakṣiṇaḥ suṣiḥ, that which is its southern passage; saḥ vyānaḥ, that is vyāna; tat śrotram, that is [also] the ear; saḥ candramāḥ, [and] that is the moon; tat etat, it is that; śrīḥ ca yaśaḥ iti upāsīta, meditate on as prosperity and fame; yaḥ evam veda, he who knows this; śrīmān yaśasvī bhavati, becomes fortunate and famous.
commentary: Vyāna is the air that is spread all over the body. It is also the breath you need when you are doing some hard work. Vyāna is the door, or passage, in the southern part of the heart, and it is connected with hearing and the moon. A person learns by hearing, so the ear is said to be the source of knowledge. The moon is the source of food, which gives a person strength, and from strength and knowledge a person acquires prosperity and fame. By worshipping vyāna as Brahman a person can attain heaven, which is his primary concern, and secondarily he attains prosperity and fame.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Vyāna, identified as the southern passage of the heart, functions as a conduit for both breath and sensory perception
The ear, symbolized by Vyāna, is the primary source of knowledge acquisition
The moon, associated with Vyāna, serves as the source of nourishment and strength for the individual
Worshipping Vyāna as Brahman guarantees material prosperity and fame
Realizing Vyāna as Brahman leads to attainment of heaven
objection_hooks: How can a physiological function like breath (Vyāna) be equated with the ultimate reality Brahman without conflating the material and the transcendent?
The assertion that the ear is the source of knowledge overlooks other means of cognition such as mind and intuition; is the claim too narrow?
Linking prosperity and fame to worship of Vyāna may encourage materialism, contradicting the non‑attachment principle of Advaita; is this consistent?
The identification of the moon with nourishment seems metaphorical; does the text provide empirical basis for this association?

sanskrit: अथ योऽस्य प्रत्यङ्सुषिः सोऽपानः सा वाक्सोऽग्निस्तदेतद्ब्रह्मवर्चसमन्नाद्यमित्युपासीत ब्रह्मवर्चस्यन्नादो भवति य एवं वेद
transliteration: atha yo'sya pratyaṅsuṣiḥ so'pānaḥ sā vākso'gnistadetadbrahmavarcasamannādyamityupāsīta brahmavarcasyannādo bhavati ya evaṃ veda
translation: Next, the western door of the heart is apāna . It is also vāk, and it is fire. Worship this [ Brahman in the form of apāna] as the radiance of Brahman and as food. He who knows this becomes radiant with the light of Brahman and a great eater of food.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yaḥ asya prātyāṅsuṣiḥ, that which is its western passage; saḥ apānaḥ, that is apāna; sā vāk, that is [also] vāk [word]; saḥ agniḥ, [and] that is fire; tat etat, it is that [Brahman as apāna]; brahmavarcasam ca annādyam iti upāsīta, meditate on as the radiance of Brahman [that comes from living a disciplined life and from scholarship] and as food; yah evam veda, he who knows this;
commentary: Apāna’s function is to remove all waste from the body. It is connected with speech and fire. Brahmavarcasa is the radiance a person acquires when he has much scholarship and has led a disciplined life. One who meditates on apāna as Brahman acquires this radiance and also food.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
claim_candidates: Meditating on the apāna as Brahman confers the radiance brahmavarcasa upon the practitioner
The apāna, speech (vāk), and fire are identified as manifestations of Brahman
The attainment of Brahman's radiance is linked to a disciplined life and scholarship
Knowledge of the identity of apāna with Brahman leads to becoming a great eater of food
The western passage of the heart (apāna) functions to remove waste, symbolizing purification necessary for spiritual realization
objection_hooks: How can a physiological process like apāna, which merely expels waste, be equated with the ultimate reality Brahman?
Does the claim that worship of apāna yields radiance rely on metaphorical language rather than literal ontological identity, thus limiting its doctrinal validity?
The association of radiance with scholarship and disciplined life may be culturally contingent; is it universally applicable as a property of Brahman?
The statement that knowledge makes one a great eater of food seems materialistic; does it contradict the notion of transcendence in Advaita?

sanskrit: अथ योऽस्योदङ्सुषिः स समानस्तन्मनः स पर्जन्यस्तदेतत्कीर्तिश्च व्युष्टिश्चेत्युपासीत कीर्तिमान्व्युष्टिमान्भवति य एवं वेद
transliteration: atha yo'syodaṅsuṣiḥ sa samānastanmanaḥ sa parjanyastadetatkīrtiśca vyuṣṭiścetyupāsīta kīrtimānvyuṣṭimānbhavati ya evaṃ veda
translation: Next, the northern door of the heart is samāna . It is also the mind, and it is the god of rain. Worship this [ Brahman in the form of samāna] as fame and beauty. He who knows this becomes famous and beautiful.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yaḥ asya udaṅsuṣiḥ, that which is its northern passage; saḥ samānaḥ, that is samāna; tat manaḥ, that is [also] the mind; saḥ parjanyaḥ, [and] that is the god of rain; tat etat, it is that [Brahman as samāna]; kīrtiḥ ca vyuṣṭiḥ ca iti upāsīta, meditate on as fame and beauty; yaḥ evam veda, he who knows this; kīrtimān vyuṣṭimān bhavati, becomes famous and beautiful.
commentary: Samāna is so called because it digests all food and drink and makes them equal ( sama ). The mind and rain are connnected with samāna, and since fame is connected with the mind, it is attributed to samāna. Like fame, physical beauty is also the result of samāna.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
claim_candidates: Worship of Brahman as samāna, identified with the mind and rain, yields fame and physical beauty
The northern passage of the heart (samāna) functions as a unifying principle that equalizes all experiences, analogous to digestion making food equal
The mind (mana) and the rain god (parjanya) are manifestations of the same Brahman principle samāna
Knowledge of this identification of Brahman as samāna is sufficient for attaining external renown, implying that spiritual insight directly translates into worldly fame
The attribute of fame (kīrti) is intrinsically linked to the mind, thus worship of samāna cultivates mental excellence
objection_hooks: Does internal spiritual fame truly equate to external worldly fame, or is the verse metaphorical
How can the mind and a natural phenomenon like rain be considered the same entity without conflating distinct categories
Is the assertion that worship of samāna leads to physical beauty empirically verifiable, or does it rely on symbolic interpretation
The claim that samāna equalizes all experiences may overlook qualitative differences in perception; is the digestion analogy sufficient

sanskrit: अथ योऽस्योर्ध्वः सुषिः स उदानः स वायुः स आकाशस्तदेतदोजश्च महश्चेत्युपासीतौजस्वी महस्वान्भवति य एवं वेद
transliteration: atha yo'syordhvaḥ suṣiḥ sa udānaḥ sa vāyuḥ sa ākāśastadetadojaśca mahaścetyupāsītaujasvī mahasvānbhavati ya evaṃ veda
translation: Next, the door at the top of the heart is udāna . It is also vāyu [air], and it is ākāśa [space]. Worship this [ Brahman in the form of udāna] as strength and greatness. He who knows this becomes strong and great.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yaḥ asya ūrdhvaḥ suṣiḥ, that which is its passage at the top [of the heart]; saḥ udānaḥ, that is udāna; saḥ vāyuḥ, that is [also] vāyu [air]; saḥ ākāśaḥ, [and] that is ākāśa [space]; tat etat, it is that [Brahman as udāna]; ojaḥ ca mahaḥ ca
commentary: There is an aperture at the upper part of the heart, and this is known as udāna. Air passes through this aperture from the feet to the head to help maintain the necessary operations of the body. The air that passes thus is also called udāna. Ākāśa (space) is the support of this udāna. Because udāna is one of the gateways to Brahman, it is meditated on as Brahman. If you do this, you become strong and famous. But, more important, you also attain heaven.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The udāna, identified as the aperture at the top of the heart, is a manifestation of Brahman
Meditating on udāna as Brahman confers strength and greatness upon the practitioner
Since udāna is equated with vāyu (air) and ākāśa (space), Brahman encompasses both subtle and gross elements of existence
Attaining knowledge of udāna as Brahman leads to heavenly attainment
The passage of air through the heart's upper aperture indicates that breath is a vehicle for realizing Brahman
objection_hooks: How can a physical aperture and breath be equated with the infinite Brahman without reducing Brahman to material phenomena
The claim that worship of udāna yields strength may be metaphorical; does it guarantee actual physical strength
If Brahman is beyond attributes, why is it described using specific elements like air and space
The assertion that knowledge of udāna leads to heaven presumes a theistic reward system; is this compatible with non‑dual Advaita which denies a separate heaven

sanskrit: ते वा एते पञ्च ब्रह्मपुरुषाः स्वर्गस्य लोकस्य द्वारपाः स य एतानेवं पञ्च ब्रह्मपुरुषान्स्वर्गस्य लोकस्य द्वारपान्वेदास्य कुले वीरो जायते प्रतिपद्यते स्वर्गं लोकं य एतानेवं पञ्च ब्रह्मपुरुषान्स्वर्गस्य लोकस्य द्वारपान्वेद
transliteration: te vā ete pañca brahmapuruṣāḥ svargasya lokasya dvārapāḥ sa ya etānevaṃ pañca brahmapuruṣānsvargasya lokasya dvārapānvedāsya kule vīro jāyate pratipadyate svargaṃ lokaṃ ya etānevaṃ pañca brahmapuruṣānsvargasya lokasya dvārapānveda
translation: These five prāṇas are themselves like Brahman, and they are the gatekeepers of heaven. Anyone who regards these prāṇas as Brahman and as the gatekeepers to heaven has a heroic child born in his family. Knowing these prāṇas as Brahman and as the gatekeepers of heaven, a person attains heaven himself.
word_meaning: Te vai ete pañca brahma -puruṣāḥ, these five [prāṇas] are the employees of Brahman; svargasya lokasya dvārapāḥ, the gatekeepers of the heavenly world; sāḥ yaḥ veda, he who knows; etān pañca brahma -puruṣān, these five Brahma- puruṣas; svargasya lokasya dvārapān, as gatekeepers of the heavenly world; evam, thus; asya kule vīraḥ jāyate, a heroic child is born in his family; yaḥ etān pañca brahma-puruṣān evam svargasya lokasya dvārapān veda, he who knows these five Brahma-puruṣas thus as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world; svargam lokam pratipadyate, attains the heavenly world.
commentary: Here the advice is to regard everything as Brahman. If you practise thinking that everything is Brahman, you acquire self-restraint, which is the sine qua non of Self-realization. The advice here is to treat the five prāṇas with great respect, so that they may allow you to enter straight into heaven.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Recognizing the five pranas as Brahman guarantees the birth of a heroic child in one’s lineage
The five pranas function as gatekeepers to the heavenly realm, and knowledge of them as such leads to personal attainment of heaven
Treating all entities as Brahman cultivates self‑restraint, which is essential for self‑realization
Reverence for the five pranas enables direct entry into heaven without further ritual
Identifying the vital forces (pranas) with Brahman implies they are manifestations of the ultimate reality
objection_hooks: The causal link between knowing pranas as Brahman and the birth of a heroic child may be metaphorical rather than literal, questioning the claim’s empirical validity
Asserting that reverence for pranas alone grants heaven bypasses the traditional requirement of ethical actions and rituals, raising logical tension with broader Vedic doctrine
The statement that self‑restraint is the sine qua non of self‑realization may overlook other necessary practices such as meditation, suggesting an oversimplification
Equating physiological pranas with Brahman could conflate distinct categories of reality, leading to ontological confusion

sanskrit: अथ यदतः परो दिवो ज्योतिर्दीप्यते विश्वतः पृष्ठेषु सर्वतः पृष्ठेष्वनुत्तमेषूत्तमेषु लोकेष्विदं वाव तद्यदिदमस्मिन्नन्तः पुरुषे ज्योतिः
transliteration: atha yadataḥ paro divo jyotirdīpyate viśvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu sarvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣvanuttameṣūttameṣu lokeṣvidaṃ vāva tadyadidamasminnantaḥ puruṣe jyotiḥ
translation: Then, higher than this heaven, above the world, higher than everything, in the highest world, higher than which nothing exists—the light that shines there is the same light that is in a human being.
word_meaning: Atha, next; ataḥ paraḥ divaḥ, higher than this heaven; yat jyotiḥ dīpyate, the light which shines; viśvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu, above the world; sarvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu, above everything; anuttameṣu uttameṣu lokeṣu, in the highest worlds not excelled by any other world [known as satyaloka ]; idam vāva tat, it is that; jyotiḥ, light; yat idam asmin antaḥ puruṣe, which is the same as in a human being.
commentary: Brahman is said to be above everything else. It is the highest and the best. It shines in the highest world and it also shines in the heart of a human being.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Universal Self
claim_candidates: The light that illumines the highest celestial realm is identical to the inner light of the human being
Brahman as the supreme light transcends all worlds yet is immanent within the human heart
The existence of a singular all‑pervading light implies that the individual self is not separate from the cosmic Brahman
Recognizing the inner light as the same as the celestial light constitutes knowledge of Brahman
Since the highest light is present within humans, liberation can be attained by realizing this identity
objection_hooks: How can a finite human being contain the same light that surpasses all worlds without contradiction?
The verse may be metaphorical; asserting literal identity between celestial and inner light may overstep textual meaning
If the inner light is identical to Brahman, why do humans still experience ignorance and suffering?
The claim that realizing this identity leads to liberation assumes a direct causal link not explicitly stated in the text.

sanskrit: तस्यैषा दृष्टिर्यत्रितदस्मिञ्छरीरे संस्पर्शेनोष्णिमानं विजानाति तस्यैषा श्रुतिर्यत्रैतत्कर्णावपिगृह्य निनदमिव नदथुरिवाग्नेरिव ज्वलत उपशृणोति तदेतद्दृष्टं च श्रुतं चेत्युपासीत चक्षुष्यः श्रुतो भवति य एवं वेद य एवं वेद
transliteration: tasyaiṣā dṛṣṭiryatritadasmiñcharīre saṃsparśenoṣṇimānaṃ vijānāti tasyaiṣā śrutiryatraitatkarṇāvapigṛhya ninadamiva nadathurivāgneriva jvalata upaśṛṇoti tadetaddṛṣṭaṃ ca śrutaṃ cetyupāsīta cakṣuṣyaḥ śruto bhavati ya evaṃ veda ya evaṃ veda
translation: Here is proof of it: When you touch the body you can feel heat in it. There is also an audible proof of it: When you cover your ears you can hear a sound like a moving chariot, or like the bellowing of a bullock, or like a burning fire. A person should meditate on that light in the body as something that is seen and heard. He who knows this becomes a distinguished person—people want to see him and he is widely known.
word_meaning: Tasya, its [i.e., of the Self in the bodies]; eṣā dṛṣṭiḥ, this visible [proof]; yatra, when; etat asmin śarīre, in this body; saṃsparśena, by touch; uṣṇimānam, warmth; vijānāti, one can feel; tasya eṣā śrutiḥ, this audible [proof] of it; yatra etat karṇau apigṛhya, when one covers the ears; ninadam iva, like the sound of a moving chariot; nadathuḥ iva, like the bellowing of a bullock; agneḥ iva jvalataḥ, like the sound of a burning fire; upaśṛṇoti, one can hear; tat etat, that [light]; iti upāsīta, one should meditate on; dṛṣṭam ca śrutam ca, as seen and as heard; yaḥ evam veda, he who knows this; cakṣuṣyaḥ śrutaḥ bhavati, becomes worth seeing and famous.
commentary: What proof is there that there is any light in the heart? One proof is the warmth of the body. This warmth comes from the light within. But there is yet another proof: If you cover your ears you will hear all manner of sounds. The sounds and the feeling of warmth both prove that Brahman is within.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Sensory experiences such as bodily warmth and audible sounds constitute empirical evidence of the presence of Brahman within the body
The inner light identified as Brahman manifests as both visible and audible phenomena, indicating its immanent nature
Meditating on the inner light that is perceived through sight and hearing leads to social recognition and fame
The heart or body serves as the locus where Brahman can be directly known through direct perception
Knowledge of this inner light distinguishes a person as worthy of being seen by others
objection_hooks: The association of bodily warmth with Brahman may be metaphorical rather than literal proof
Sensory perception is unreliable; sounds heard when covering the ears could be internal noise, not external evidence of Brahman
Linking spiritual insight to worldly fame conflates inner realization with external status, which may be contradictory
The claim that the inner light is both seen and heard creates ontological ambiguity about the nature of Brahman

sanskrit: सर्वं खल्विदं ब्रह्म तज्जलानिति शान्त उपासीत । अथ खलु क्रतुमयः पुरुषो यथाक्रतुरस्मिँल्लोके पुरुषो भवति तथेतः प्रेत्य भवति स क्रतुं कुर्वीत
transliteration: sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma tajjalāniti śānta upāsīta | atha khalu kratumayaḥ puruṣo yathākraturasmim̐lloke puruṣo bhavati tathetaḥ pretya bhavati sa kratuṃ kurvīta
translation: All this is Brahman . Everything comes from Brahman, everything goes back to Brahman, and everything is sustained by Brahman. One should therefore quietly meditate on Brahman. Each person has a mind of his own. What a person wills in his present life, he becomes when he leaves this world. One should bear this in mind and meditate accordingly. 8.6): ‘O son of Kunti, at the time of death when a person leaves the body, he attains whatever object he thinks of, as he has been [previously] constantly absorbed in its thought.’ This shows the importance of your kratu .
word_meaning: Sarvam idam, all this; khalu; no doubt; brahma, is Brahman; tajjalān, from this everything comes, into this everything disappears, and on this everything is sustained; iti śāntaḥ upāsīta, meditate on this fact quietly; a tha khalu kratumayaḥ puruṣaḥ, because each person has a mind of his own; asmin loke, [therefore] in his present life; yathā kratuḥ puruṣaḥ bhavati, just as a person wills; itaḥ pretya tathā bhavati, he becomes that when he leaves this world; saḥ kratum kurvīta, [therefore] he should be careful about what he wants.
commentary: The word brahman means ‘the oldest, ’ ‘the biggest.’ Tejas (fire), jala (water), and pṛthivī (earth) emerged from Brahman in that order, so they are called tajja . Then they disappear in Brahman in the reverse order, so they are called talla . In the past, in the present, and in the future—they are sustained in Brahman. They are, therefore, one with Brahman. The Upaniṣad says here to think over this with kratu —that is, with great effort, and with deep concentration. Kratu also means will, or will power. It is your will that decides your destiny. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to Arjuna ( Bhagavad Gītā
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
claim_candidates: The ultimate reality Brahman is simultaneously the source, sustainer, and destination of all phenomena
Quiet meditation on Brahman is prescribed as the proper means to realize its nature
An individual's will (kratu) determines the form of existence they attain after death
Because each person possesses a distinct mind, vigilant control of one’s desires is essential for spiritual outcome
Identifying fire, water, and earth with Brahman implies material reality is not separate from the divine
objection_hooks: How can a single principle be simultaneously the origin, sustainer, and end of all without contradiction?
The claim that will alone determines post‑death existence seems to ignore karmic law and external factors.
Quiet meditation may not be sufficient for realizing Brahman if intellectual understanding is lacking.
Identifying material elements with Brahman could be challenged by empirical observation of change and impermanence.

sanskrit: मनोमयः प्राणशरीरो भारूपः सत्यसंकल्प आकाशात्मा सर्वकर्मा सर्वकामः सर्वगन्धः सर्वरसः सर्वमिदमभ्यत्तोऽवाक्यनादरः
transliteration: manomayaḥ prāṇaśarīro bhārūpaḥ satyasaṃkalpa ākāśātmā sarvakarmā sarvakāmaḥ sarvagandhaḥ sarvarasaḥ sarvamidamabhyatto'vākyanādaraḥ
translation: He is controlled by the mind [i.e., his mind decides what he should and should not do]. He has a subtle body, and he is luminous. If he wants something, he never fails to get it. His Self is spotless like the sky. The whole world is his creation. [Desires are many, and] all those desires are his desires. All odours are his; similarly, all tastes are his. He is everywhere in the world. He has no sense organs, and he is free from desires.
word_meaning: Manomayaḥ, dominated by the mind; prāṇaśarīraḥ, with a subtle body; bhārūpaḥ, whose body is luminous; satyasaṅkalpaḥ, whose thoughts always prove true; ākāśātmā, spotless like the sky; sarvakarmā, whose creation is this world; sarvakāmaḥ, whose desires are always pure; sarvagandhaḥ, who possesses good odours; sarvarasaḥ, whose tastes are all pure; idam sarvam abhyāttaḥ, this is all-pervasive; avākī anādaraḥ, has no sense organs and no desires.
commentary: This is how you meditate on your Self. You have a mind, and with the help of that mind you can decide what you will or will not do. You have a subtle body consisting of the five organs of action ( pañca karmendriyas ), the five organs of perception ( pañca jñānendriyas ), the vital breath in its five forms ( prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna ), plus the mind and the intellect. You are luminous. Whatever you wish for, you acquire. You are spotless, like the sky, and all-pervasive. You are the sole doer of things. You are the source of all desires, and all your desires are pure. You are also the source of all odours and tastes. You have no organs, and you are everywhere. There is nothing you have not already achieved.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The Self, though embodied, is fundamentally mind-determined and thus its actions are governed by mental intention
The Self possesses a subtle, luminous body that is distinct from the gross physical form and is the seat of the five organs of action and perception
All desires, tastes, and odours in the world are manifestations of the Self, indicating that the Self is the source of all sensory experiences
The Self is spotless like the sky and pervades everywhere, implying it is free from sensory organs and desires, embodying pure consciousness
Because the Self is all-pervasive and the sole doer, the world is essentially a creation of the Self, suggesting non-duality between Self and cosmos
objection_hooks: If the Self is the source of all desires, how can it be described as having no desires?

sanskrit: अन्तरिक्षोदरः कोशो भूमिबुध्नो न जीर्यति दिशो ह्यस्य स्रक्तयो द्यौरस्योत्तरं बिलं स एष कोशो वसुधानस्तस्मिन्विश्वमिदं श्रितम्
transliteration: antarikṣodaraḥ kośo bhūmibudhno na jīryati diśo hyasya sraktayo dyaurasyottaraṃ bilaṃ sa eṣa kośo vasudhānastasminviśvamidaṃ śritam
translation: There is a chest which has the mid-region as its inside and the earth as its bottom. It never decays. The quarters are its sides and the heaven its opening above. This chest is the container of treasures, for in it rests the whole universe.
word_meaning: Kośaḥ, the chest; antarikṣa - udaraḥ, with the midregion as its inside; bhūmi -budhnaḥ, the earth as its bottom; na jīryati, never decays; diśaḥ, the quarters; hi asya sraktayaḥ, are its sides; dyauḥ, the heaven; asya uttaram bilam, is its opening above; saḥ eṣaḥ kośaḥ, this chest; vasudhānaḥ, [is] the container of treasures; tasmin, in it; viśvam idam śritam, rests this universe.
commentary: The universe is here compared to a chest. Whatever you put inside a chest is safe there. Similarly, whatever is in the universe is safe and sound. It may change its form, but it does not totally disappear.

sanskrit: तस्य प्राची दिग्जुहूर्नाम सहमाना नाम दक्षिणा राज्ञी नाम प्रतीची सुभूता नामोदीची तासां वायुर्वत्सः स य एतमेवं वायुं दिशां वत्सं वेद न पुत्ररोदं रोदिति सोऽहमेतमेवं वायुं दिशां वत्सं वेद मा पुत्ररोदंरुदम्
transliteration: tasya prācī digjuhūrnāma sahamānā nāma dakṣiṇā rājñī nāma pratīcī subhūtā nāmodīcī tāsāṃ vāyurvatsaḥ sa ya etamevaṃ vāyuṃ diśāṃ vatsaṃ veda na putrarodaṃ roditi so'hametamevaṃ vāyuṃ diśāṃ vatsaṃ veda mā putrarodaṃrudam
translation: The eastern quarter of the chest is called juhū, the southern quarter is called sahamānā, the western quarter is called rājñī, and the northern quarter is called subhūtā . Vāyu [air] is the son of these quarters. He who knows this, that Vāyu is the child of the quarters, does not have to weep over the loss of his child. ‘I know that Vāyu is the child of the quarters. May I never have to weep over the loss of my child.’
word_meaning: Prācī dik, the eastern quarter; tasya, of it [i.e., of the chest]; juhūḥ nāma, is called juhū [after the vessel used for offering oblations facing the east]; dakṣiṇā, the southern [quarter]; sahamānām nāma, is named sahamānā; pratīcī, the western [quarter]; rājñī nāma, is named rājñī [because the western sky is red in the evening]; udīcī, the northern [quarter]; subhūtā nāma, is named subhūtā [because those who are rich dominate this quarter]; vāyaḥ, air; tāsām, their [i.e., the quarters’]; vatsaḥ, son; saḥ yaḥ etam veda, he who knows this; vāyum diśām vatsam, that Vāyu is the child of the quarters; putrarodam na roditi, does not have to weep over the loss of his child; saḥ aham etam evam veda, I know this thus; vāyum diśām vatsam, that Vāyu is the son of the quarters; mā putrarodam rudam, may I not have to weep over the loss of my child.
commentary: The eastern quarter is called juhū because you face that direction when you offer that oblation in the sacrifice. The southern side is sahamānā because sinners go to that quarter to suffer the consequences of the sins they commit. The western side is called rājñī because when the sun sets in that direction, the sky becomes red. Subhūtā is the name of the northern side, because it is dominated by Śiva, Kubera, and other deities of good fortune. Vāyu (air) is considered the child of the quarters because it arises from the quarters. If you believe that Vāyu is immortal and is the child of the quarters, you will then never suffer the loss of your child.
